MR. REYNOLDS-DISPATCHING OF CERTAIN MAIL BY HOUSE OF COMMONS POST OFFICE AS THIRD CLASS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege, of which I have given you notice, regarding the Post Office and a letter received by me on October 27 from the Postmaster General with regard to the mailing to my riding of some 5,000 pieces of mail. This mail took approximately four to five weeks to reach my constituents, which has caused me severe embarrassment.
I wrote to the Postmaster General, explained the matter to him and asked for an explanation as all these envelopes left my office franked and were delivered to the Post Office. His answer was that he understood the envelopes were all of brown Manilla, approximately 6 by 9 in size, and would have been processed and dispatched by the House of Commons Post Office as third class mail. I was quite concerned about this because I was under the impression that all mail of Members of Parliament that is franked leaves the House of Commons as first class mail.
As you know, Sir, I wrote to you and asked if this was so. Today I received a letter from you saying that this is so, that franked mail leaves the House as first class mail and only the mail of householders may be set aside as third class mail. This has disturbed me greatly and caused me embarrassment. I know that other hon. members have also been caused embarrassment.
If Your Honour agrees with me that I have a question of privilege, I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale):
That this matter be referred to the Standing Committee on Elections and Privileges.
I do so in order that the Postmaster General can be given a set of guidelines as to how mail is to leave the House of Commons and so that mail that leaves this House will be treated at least on the same basis as that of other citizens of Canada. When a letter is posted before eleven o'clock it is supposed to be delivered the next day.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. REYNOLDS-DISPATCHING OF CERTAIN MAIL BY HOUSE OF COMMONS POST OFFICE AS THIRD CLASS
speechtext:
The hon. member has given the Chair the notice required under the Standing Order, so that I have had an opportunity to consider the difficulty to which the hon. member has alluded. I assure him that I am very sorry and regret very much that he has been put to this considerable and very real embarrassment. On behalf of the staff of the House, myself and all those who may be responsible in some way for the difficulty, I apologize to the hon. member.
At the same time, my understanding from the subsequent inquiries I have made is that it has been the practice to forward by third class mail bulk mail including, more particularly, brown envelopes when they come to the post office in the thousands. It has been the practice of the Postmaster in our Post Office and his staff to consider these as third class mail unless there is a specific request by members. I was not aware of this regulation, and I feel that hon. members are entitled to have the matter looked into. It may well be, because of the large volume of mail that goes out for the purpose of serving members adequately, that the practice followed until now is one which should be followed, and if that be the case, we should certainly make sure that all hon. members are made aware of it.
I regret very much, as I said, the embarrassment caused to the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta. I will look into the matter further, if the hon. member will allow me to do so, and try to advise all hon. members as to the procedures which are followed at present and which might be improved on the basis of advice and counsel from hon. members.

speechtext:
That this House deplores the fact that the government is maintaining the unity of the country through fear, autocracy and oligarchy, and has failed to do anything to encourage the provinces to get together in order to amend or redraft the Canadian constitution, thus protecting the country against national difficulties by meeting the basic aspirations of each province.
He said: It is quite an honour for me today to put forward this serious and realistic motion on behalf of the Social Credit Party of Canada, a motion urging all hon. members to ponder over the constitutional situation in our country, in order to try and find adequate solutions which would favour both the autonomy and development of all regions of Canada.
November 8, 1973

The surprise, or rather the state of shock, which resulted from the last provincial elections in Quebec should not cause us to delude ourselves into believing that there are no problems any more, the greater majority of Quebecers having chosen the status quo, that is, the federalist option. On the contrary, the analysis of the results show that the people of Quebec, because of the fear and panic systematically nourished by Liberal governments both in Ottawa and Quebec City since 1968, have been unable to make a political choice based on the platforms of the various parties, but rather have indicated their unwillingness to decide the future of their province in an election. The Liberal strategy was pushed so far that the point was reached where the Quebec voter might fear independence more than the mob which might explain perhaps the decision to adjourn the sittings of the commission of inquiry into organized crime during the election campaign.
I must confess, Mr. Speaker, that other political parties in that province unconsciously or otherwise played the Liberal game. They involuntarily pushed part of their own supporters in that Liberal wave that nearly destroyed democracy in Quebec. I do not think that they will become again that shield, that screen, that unconscious instrument that suits those who vindicate an outdated status quo and keep the unity of this nation going through fear, autocracy and oligarchy. The Liberal government of Canada, the quiet owner of constitutional truth, seems to do away with the opinion of opposition parties. That results in a oneway dialogue between federalists and independentists. We have a government that establishes through feelings, fear and false security an authoritarian and dictatorial regime in that area.
At the time of the first colonial conferences which resulted in the BNA Act four provinces decided to form a confederation of autonomous states based on the historic circumstances at that time. The intentions of those commonly known of the Fathers of Confederation were certainly not I think those that are attributed to them at times today. Yet, it must be recognized that the federal government is only the creature of the provinces, and if 106 years later the provinces now numbering ten decide to amend or rewrite that constitution they of course have the priority and they alone may determine jointly the changes that are necessary for the benefit of all the provinces in general or each and everyone of them in particular.
The part played by the federal Parliament is therefore becoming more that of a motivator, observer and conciliator. This is obviously a far cry from that assumed by preceding governments-especially that of the present government with its arrogant paternalism-which have always refused to let the provinces have their autonomy or amend the constitution, thus compelling an impressive number of Quebecers to resort to extreme solutions.
They have forgotten that the Fathers of Confederation had wanted to make the country strong, to have a kind of common market in a position to resist the ravenous and insatiable appetite of the American ogre. It was imperative for that that French Canada remain itself, thus staying by its own originality the attacks of American imper-alism and making Canada what it is.
Constitution
We must therefore recognize, Mr. Speaker, that we are now before a fait accompli. Canadian confederation has bit by bit developed into a centralizing and unitary Canadian state.
As a consequence of all kinds of events,-economic crises, wars, and so on-the spirit of the Constitution itself has been distorted. Of course, this Constitution has become outmoded, inadequate, and is at the root of many a dispute. All across Canada, and particularly in Quebec, people are expecting changes. The need for a reform is a priority.
The government could reply that they have made a great effort, while they have found nothing better at the height of the constitutional storm than to offer, or rather to try and impose upon the provinces, in 1971, the famous Victoria Charter that all the political parties represented in the Quebec National Assembly rejected unanimously.
By its action the government has turned a national issue into a matter of political partisanship. In Quebec, if one choses to be a federalist one must indiscriminately be a Liberal. Anyone who feels strongly about the development of Quebec is called a separatist.
I remember that on several occasions, when I was sitting on the other side of the House, the Liberal members never failed to call me a separatist as soon as my observations were in favour of Quebec.
They believe that it is sentimental nationalism to struggle for the emancipation and self achievement of one's fellow citizens. I would say, Mr. Speaker, that the most sentimental are not on the side we think they are.
I find my Liberal colleagues are fond of great epic battles against separatism and they are satisfied with that because they believe that Quebecers will never give away this beautiful and great Canada which belongs to them. You believe that as long as you never cross the Ottawa River. I think they count on people's emotions. They rely on that fear of separatism and they stand on their position.
Mr. Speaker, that is the best way to exasperate progressive people in this country.
We should obviously not minimize the importance of this element since the analysis of the recent election in Quebec has shown that more than 35 per cent of the French Canadians in Quebec voted for the Parti Quebecois in spite of the devastating majority gathered by the liberal steamroller.
Mr. Speaker, it is high time that we should say whatever has to be said. Truth has been hidden too long. Let us open our hearts and minds to sincere and friendly discussion. We should no longer fear to face the problems as they really are. Canada is an adult country which can, in all honesty, let every province decide whichever amendments should be made to the Constitution, or whether it should be entirely revamped.
The federal government should be sufficiently conscientious, if not magnanimous, to admit that its excessive centralization policy has been wrong and that it should give back to the provinces the prerogatives which they demand.

November 8, 1973
Constitution
As concerns our constitutional future, Mr. Speaker, many personalities have already mentioned various alternatives. At one of the federal-provincial conferences, the former premier of British Columbia spoke of a Confederation of five regions instead of ten.
The now Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) is known to hold the same opinion. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) has often alluded to this subject. You will certainly remember his statement of November 29, 1970, in which he said:
"A referendum might be necessary because more and more the federal government is heading towards ultimate confrontation with the separatist movement" ...
This proves again how this government seems to favour and consider separatism as politically valuable.
To support my argument I would like to quote from an editorial by Jean Pellerin published in La Presse of Montreal on Tuesday November 6, 1973. Even though I do not agree with all the points raised in the editorial, I think this quotation should back up today's motion. I quote:
Canada has been considering as desirable the repatriation of its constitution and the adoption of a Canadian formula of amendment for such a long time, could it be that the time for taking this historic decision is drawing near?
In Canada, it is difficult to have everyone in agreement. The Canadian opinion is divided on several points but people do agree at least, and almost to a man, on the necessity of repatriating the constitution some day.
Agreement also exists in Quebec. The election of October 29 indicated that most people in this province do not trust separatism. But, nonetheless, this majority is not satisfied with our current constitution. On the contrary, people want a major reform. Aware of their cultural peculiarities, they want Quebec to enjoy the widest possible sovereignty but in view of the economic advantages inherent in the federal ties, they agree to dispense with an impossible absolute sovereignty and negotiate a sovereignty that would be adjusted to the common welfare of this country.
One could also quote a good deal of statements along the same lines, that would show that although in apparent stability, Canada is near the breaking point. Therefore we must come back as soon as possible to concrete autonomy principles. This party has always contended and still contends that there can be neither progress nor development without complete respect for the individual, for the human being. What is true for the individual is equally true for a community. Respect for provincial autonomy is necessary and even essential.
It is with the greatest ease that we can point that out since this party has never known any dissension in that respect. Wherever one meets Creditistes in Canada, one can observe that mutual respect for the individual character of each province. The Creditistes are a big family where everybody feel's at home, no matter where they come from; they earnestly hope that the government will at last give the example of a policy based on Social Credit economic principles. One can even believe that all Creditistes would be very happy to help and support an inde-pendentist government in any province, if Major Douglas' philosophy were implemented.
We know, Mr. Speaker, that the eventual part to be played by the Banque du Quebec in an independent Quebec could be substantially the same as the one the Social Credit Party of Canada would like to be played by

the Bank of Canada. This is neither an ultimatum nor a threat; it is a bare fact. To shut oneself in an outmoded and backward status quo is to show a blatant lack of maturity.
Let me also add to my argument the conclusion which the Chamber of Commerce of the province of Quebec came to as regards the reform of the constitution-and which is recorded in the January 1969 issue of its publication, and I quote:
"The form of federalism that we have known will have to be changed: (a) the constitution of Canada will have to be amended or redrafted in order to define clearly the responsibilities of each government level, to enable each to levy taxes to meet these responsibilities and to include a mechanism designed to efficiently prevent abuses of jurisdiction; (b) the tax policy of the federal government and that of the provinces will be developed only after consultation which will have to be of an official and permanent nature; (c) monetary and tariff policies of the federal government will have to be set up through consultation with the provinces and these consultations will also be of an official and permanent nature; (d) the Bank of Canada should facilitate the financing of provinces and through the latter, that of municipalities and school boards. 4.-French Canadians must be convinced that their development depends essentially on their dynamism in every field of the economic and social life. 5.-English Canadians will have to show by concrete measures that they totally accept French Canadians as partners and will not prevent them in any way from acceeding to management positions, in both the public and the private sectors of the economy as well as the administration of this country. It is rather a matter of attitude being shown in everyday's measures that are taken at both government and business levels and related to purchasing, professional services, promotion, advertising and other policies."
Finally the last recommendation of the Chamber of Commerce reads as follows:
"6.-The Chamber of Commerce and other organizations should carry on their studies, in order to enlighten further and constantly the people of Canada on the economic impact of the constitutional structure of our country."
Mr. Speaker, I will dwell particularly on subsections "c" and "d" of the above-mentioned paragraph 1 where it is stated:
The monetary and tariff policies of the federal government should be established in co-operation with the provinces and those consultations should also be of an official and permanent nature: the Bank of Canada should facilitate the financing of provinces and through the latter, the financing of municipalities and school boards."
I do not believe, Mr. Speaker, that we can accuse the Chambers of Commerce of being in favour of social credit, although this attitude is awfully in agreement with what we have been trying for years to make Canadians understand. The basis of the true liberty that Canadians want is this essential material security that can only arise from a logical, scientific and adequate economic system, that is social credit. I think that is the direction that all new attempts to remodel the constitution should take.
It is obvious that we all want unity in this country but it must be the outcome of respect for the independence of the component parts of Canada. Our role in this House is not to show the provinces that we are the masters, but to urge them to be themselves by helping them to better fulfil their commitments.
November 8, 1973

We can state that there would not be any national problems in Canada if no one had stirred, through all sorts of means, French-speaking Canadians against Englishspeaking Canadians, or brought about such circumstances that there seemed to be racist animosity. Yet, if there is a man in the world who cannot be accused of racism, it is the French Canadian. For centuries, he has learned to live with other ethnic groups and never or almost never showed racist feelings. Of course, he feels that noble pride arising from a sound nationalism. Our English-speaking friends can certainly not blame him for it since it is because of him that Canada is what it is, that is a distinct entity from the United States.
The more the French Canadian will remain himself, the more his fellow countrymen throughout the country will benefit from it.
Quebecers or French Canadians do appreciate their English-speaking fellow countrymen and all new Canadians; only the Liberal government political action tends, purposely or not, to maintain a pernicious animosity in opposing federalists against separatists.
We have too many serious and urgent problems to settle to keep diluting them in a constitutional dead-end. Let our ethnic differences rather be useful for our mutual enrichment. We cannot however consider that it is only a matter of bread and butter; feelings have their place in every society as an individual cannot live and be happy if he never feels anything.
This minor problem set by the constitutional limits can become-and maybe is already-a major problem, because of the injustices which the French Canadians have suffered for too many years. Acts of contrition and to admission of these facts are not sufficient. In addition to filling these gaps, we must further the real emancipation and the complete development of Canada. Thus, we will objectively and positively consider all the solutions which could make us achieve the end we are seeking. These constitutional matters should therefore be debated and solved without partisanship.
These words may sound tinged with bitterness, Mr. Speaker, following the results of the October 29 election in the province of Quebec. I would answer that it is my duty to mention these circumstances to let the Canadian people know all the consequences of this new situation of democracy in my province.
Let me quote once again from a leading article by Jean-Claude Leclerc published in the November 2, 1973 issue of Le Devoir.
But worse than the distorsion which has victimized both the PQ and the CP is the absence of any sound opposition since 1970 and the continuation of a democratic deficiency; that is what should retain our attention today. After four years of complete freedom, Robert Bourassa's Liberals were due for a sound opposition to challenge them. Nothing of the sort happened. Instead, there will be less parliamentary opposition than ever to do it.
The Premier's modesty, the firm resolve indicated by some ministers not to take advantage of the situation may comfort those who are satisfied with words and promises in place of action and evidence. During their first mandate, no Liberal member, no minister could stop being hounded by scavengers and friends of the regime for contracts and jobs. After October 29, the pack will simply be bigger and will have grown bolder by the strength of the victory. That is the first conclusion to be drawn from the Liberal landslide. Unchallenged by any strong opposition, this
Constitution
government will sink faster and deeper into the "sea of power". Independence being more frightening than the underworld, there is good reason to think that neither the next election nor the one after will give us the means to control this government.
This situation could very well be disastrous if a good many of those who advocate independence lose faith in the value of democracy. But I will not labour the point.
Before I conclude, I would like the House to realize that the goal of our motion is constructive and realistic. It is clear that we cannot solve our problems if we are to count exclusively on the fear of separatism like the liberal governments of Quebec and Ottawa do. It was high time that this should be said, particularly in this House, so that all of us will be objective and realistic enough to discuss these questions.
May the discussion on this motion be of some benefit to all my fellow citizens of Quebec and Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I read the motion of the hon. member for Champlain very carefully (Mr. Matte), and also listened with great attention to his speech in which he urged the parties to co-operate and foster good feeling.
Upon reading what he said about the reopening of the constitutional debate, I think that he should have chosen words better suited to feelings of understanding instead of terms such as "fear", "autocracy", "oligarchy", in respect of present federal-provincial relations. The government of the province of Quebec did not try to squash the opposition and to reduce it to silence, it is the people of the province of Quebec who decided. They have understood that Liberals have always been in Quebec as well as elsewhere in Canada the spokesmen of one policy: a strong Quebec in an united Canada. We always stood behind that philosophy in Quebec as well as in any part of Canada.
When they speak about national unity, the Liberals never try to create discord among Canadians.

I went myself quite often to Alberta where I talked about the Canadian unity. I spoke in French in Edmonton and Calgary and I must say that I talk about Alberta with a particular interest because I am half Albertan on my mother's side. Nobody in the cabinet has more interest in Alberta than I have because I have 25 cousins there.
All across Canada we always spoke only about one thing: the importance of having a clear and unique policy throughout the country. I hear the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte) say in this House that a party is accused of being separatist if it recommends a Creditist policy inside a province. This is why the people did not vote for the Creditists at the last election in the province of Quebec. It was because of a consistent ambiguity in the creditist views. We Liberals have had the same stand from the day of Mackenzie to those of St-Laurent, Pearson, King, Laurier and the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau); we always preached the respect of every Canadian's right and particularly the linguistic rights of the French Canadians. The hon. member said that the constitutional discussion should resume. We agree with that.
7658

November 8, 1973
Constitution
But he should let the provinces take action in this field. He should remember that in 1967 Ontario premier John Robarts and Quebec premier Daniel Johnson decided to hold a provincial conference as the one proposed by the hon. member. At the end of the first conference held in Toronto, the provincial premiers asked the federal government to go back with them to the table and try to give a thrust to the constitutional debate.
After numerous discussions, we almost reached an agreement but in Victoria, at the last minute, Quebec decided not to go along. However, if the Quebec premier has any new suggestion to make, the Prime Minister said it, we will not insist on holding a new constitutional conference but we will be pleased to answer the call because we believe that some basic things must be changed in Canada such as, for instance, the inclusion in the constitution of the Bill of Rights, in order to guarantee linguistic equality and the other rights of citizens.
We Liberals believe that it is abnormal to have to go to London in order to get the constitution amended and that it would be desirable to have an entirely Canadian constitution which could be amended by the provinces or the Canadian government.
Those are known policies and if the Quebec government and the other provincial governments want to resume the constitutional debate, we are prepared to participate.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ENCOURAGE PROVINCIAL CONSULTATION TO REDRAFT THE CONSTITUTION
speechtext: Then, resume it now!

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development

speechtext:
No, because if we do so, the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) and his colleague the hon. member for Champlain, would blame us for imposing our will on the provinces but we are prepared to meet their initiatives.
It was my pleasure to note during the election campaign that when premier Bourassa, who had no policy between two stools as the creditists and the Union nationale, was speaking about viable federalism and a strong Quebec within confederation his platform included resuming the constitutional debate.
If the Quebec premier wants to resume talks on this matter the prime minister of Canada will gladly meet his initiative but we have no intention of imposing our views on any provincial government whatsoever.
However, we should be aware of the fact that the protection of the rights of French Canadians and even of the province of Quebec does not consist in always meeting the provincial representations. The federal government has a role to play as we can see today. In fact, in the debate on energy in Canada, for instance, the federal government has a role to play. In my opinion, it is essential for the Canadian government to take the necessary steps to protect all Canadians against crisis such as the energy crisis.
I am convinced that all Canadians agree on the fact that electricity, oil and other natural resources must be shared by all Canadians first and foremost. If we find we have enough, we can allow exports to other countries.
This does not only apply to Alberta oil, but also to the hydroelectrical resources that Quebec can produce, as well as to the development possibilities of Northern Canada, which first of all should benefit all Canadians.

And now that we are in the hands of the Arab States and other countries as regards energy, I would find it scandalous if the Canadian government who is responsible did not take the necessary means to ensure that in case of a more serious crisis in Canada, Alberta oil is used in Ontario, Quebec and the Maritime provinces, because we are all of us Canadians. This is why there is a Confederation. As the federal government, we must discharge our responsibilities in such matters.

No, it is wrong to say that Quebec has refused it. As a matter of fact, after the federal government announced in August that it intended to build a pipeline from Sarnia to Montreal, the provincial government issued a press release a few days ago in which it recognized that it could be essential that such a pipeline be built so that Quebec may have security of supply. And it is in the national interest that we are thinking of carrying out this project, because we would be accused of gross negligence if during the winter, in two or three years from now, for reasons of international politics, none of the countries like Venezuela or the Middle East countries wanted to move oil to Quebec or the Maritime provinces.
And if in the event of such a crisis, we had not built a pipeline from Sarnia to Montreal, we would be accused of not having fulfilled our natural obligations. However, discussions are presently going on with the Quebec government and I know for a fact that the Quebec government understands that it is the role of the federal government to make sure that Canadian energy serves all Canadians first. And I am convinced that if in the constitutional discussions or disagreements there may be between the provincial and the federal governments, being a good Canadian means always saying yes to all provincial governments, a time will come when this country will no longer exist.
What makes me a little impatient is that some people say they want a strong and united Canada and use all their energy to destroy this country. When I hear in the House of Commons of Canada a member state that if a province proposes a Creditiste program and that Credi-tiste program is related to a separatist program, he will side with them, I say he is a separatist and I will say so in all of the provinces in Canada. The Creditiste theory might be good, but I think that associating separatism with creditism is the sort of mixture that led to the rejection of creditism by Quebec voters in the last election.
We want the province to be strong within Confederation in areas that come under its jurisdiction. We have on several occasions taken clearcut action that displeased many people in Canada. For example, for years now, we have been under pressure exerted by some provinces to have more direct federal government intervention in the field of education. We always said that we must respect the provinces' jurisdiction in such matters, because we believe that education is something essential in Quebec, in order to enable the French-speaking Canadians of that province to free themselves. We have undertaken discus-
November 8, 1973

sions in a number of areas where we clearly determined certain fields of jurisdiction. For instance, family allowances. This is a problem that has been negotiated to the satisfaction of Quebec as well as that of the federal government and the other provinces. Today, we have set up an improved system of family allowances, without infringing on any provincial prerogatives.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that if the hon. member wants to contribute to improving federal-provincial relations, he should be a little more objective and stop trying to solve the problem by answering yes whenever a province asks for something. We do not intend to force the provinces to do anything in any particular area and we never will. We remain open to dialogue, and whenever the government of Quebec or any other province wants to try, together with all Canadians, to give us a new constitution or improve some clauses of the present Canadian Constitution, we will be pleased to consider it. I suggest that it is not for the federal government to take the initiative at this time. We must do what we always did, namely respond to initiatives taken by the provinces.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to come back to the statement of the hon. member for Champlain-that shocked me a little: he says that in Quebec, independence is feared more than the underworld. During the last election, this matter was not raised and I suggest that it is very unfair to the provincial government to say that they put on the shelf the inquiry on organized crime during the election campaign.
Everybody knows that it was an inquiry carried out by the courts that decided themselves that it was irrelevant to hold this public debate during an electoral campaign.
And the premier of the province of Quebec stated clearly that he had never interfered and that it is quite indecent to suggest that he might have interfered in this matter.
If the people of the province of Quebec have massively voted for the Liberal party and Premier Bourassa, it is because the latter has done what we are doing throughout Canada; he said that the Liberal party favours a united Canada that respects provinces, that federalism had to bring about advantages, that it might help poor provinces thanks to the revenues coming from wealthy provinces, for the richest provinces have often become wealthy because they have had other provinces as captive markets.
As for me, I would rather be in the position of Ontario which must pay without receiving any equalization payment, than in the position of Quebec, which receives equalization payments.
I believe each province considering the geographical features or exceptional economic developments due to the federation, have the responsibility of helping the provinces that have less. And such has been our policy for a long time, as far as family allowances are concerned, for instance. We did not want to give the whole jurisdiction to provincial governments, because with a system under which family allowances, payments of all kinds made to individuals would be the strict responsibility of the provinces, it might happen that in time the poorest provinces would be the ones to pay.
It could be that with a direct tax transfer today, the provinces could provide the same kind of service, but we
Constitution
know, for instance, that one point in corporate taxes brings twice as much in dollars to Ontario than to Quebec. Everytime a corporate tax point is given back to the provinces, Quebec loses. In the long range, Quebec is the loser because twice as much money goes into the coffers of the Ontario government as in those of the Quebec government. And with a system like that, should payments to individuals be administered by the provinces only, the situation would be such that in 10 or 15 years from now, for instance, family allowances in Newfoundland, instead of being $20, would perhaps be $10 and in Ontario, instead of being $20, they would be $40.
Now that is not the distributive justice that should exist in a confederation such as ours. That is why, Mr. Speaker,
I believe the French Canadians in the province of Quebec, last week, understood all these things.
If we really insist on raising the problem of independence, let's do it. The Liberals did not ask for this problem. It was rather a political party of the province of Quebec that keeps on preaching this thesis, while we, the Liberals, in opposition to some Creditiste members, we are not sitting on the fence with regard to independence: we are against independence.
We shall keep on fighting independence because we have the firm conviction that French Canadians can play a part at the national level, in Canada. We are not inhibited to the point where we must keep to ourselves. On the contrary, we believe that people from Quebec can be useful to all Canadians.
I am privileged to be in charge of a department which has very few contacts with the province of Quebec, but it is my profound conviction that I play a useful part not only for Quebecers but for all Canadians and this is what the federal government and Canada mean for all Quebecers.
I do not think that being a Quebecer should necessarily mean staying alone in one's back yard with one's own little things. One must have enough self-confidence to take up challenges greater than the province of Quebec. At a time when all European countries are setting up a large common market, at a time when countries throughout the world are trying to regroup in a new union-countries of the third world held an extremely important conference in Algeria a couple of weeks ago to try and regroup too-we in Quebec would be going completely against history in trying to have our little country of our own, with our own national anthem and our own flag. There is more than that to the life of a nation. I think that the important thing for us is to make sure that French Canadians can fulfill themselves not only in Quebec but everywhere in Canada.
I heard on television a few days ago that our fellow countrymen in New Brunswick were celebrating the 10th anniversay of the University of Moncton. I will point out to the hon. member for Champlain that those people are yet better French Canadians than anyone of us from the province of Quebec because they found it much more difficult to keep their French language. I refuse to go along with anybody ready to let down the million and a half French Canadians living outside Quebec. I have a lot more respect for those who lived and fought for their

In any event, Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to go on very long. I think I have clearly stated that the Quebec population made its choice. It decided by itself and it was not the federal government, because we, the federal Liberals, have showed more respect for Quebecers than did the federal Creditist members. Since we were accused in 1970 of having influenced the result of the vote, we did not interfere in the last provincial elections. Yet, the Liberal party won 102 seats out of 110. Obviously within two weeks, some intellectuals particularly in the province of Quebec will demonstrate that Rene Levesque did effectively win the election and that Mr. Bourassa lost his deposit. Mr. Speaker, the people made their choice. Every party got the same opportunity in every district. But as one of the parties offered a clear choice that met the very aspirations of French Canadians-that is to say the policy of a party which had faith in a strong Quebec in a united Canada-the people voted for that; they did not vote for the Creditist party because of the Creditist or separatist ambiguities advocated by the hon. member for Champlain. That was so obvious that the hon. member with his usual ambiguities went to his constituency to try and explain theories which are neither fish nor flesh. The Creditist candidates have lost their deposit in the ridings of Port-neuf and Laviolette and even the party president lost his in Champlain.
The Quebec voters have shown good judgment during the last election. A majority of French Canadians have voted for the Liberal party much more than for the Parti Quebecois even though, in my opinion, all those who voted for the Parti Quebecois are not necessarily separatists. I think the vote was quite clear even though some problems still exist. I am convinced that the Bourassa government will try to make some progress in many areas and that they are considering resuming the constitutional debate; we shall be open to their views because we sincerely believe that the Canadian constitution should be repa-

triated as soon as possible. In my opinion, we should find a formula of amendment meeting the aspirations of all the provinces and, at the same time, include the Canadian Bill of Rights in the Canadian constitution.
We can congratulate ourselves for the outcome of the Quebec election and we can now undertake a serious debate which will settle many problems in Canada. In the near future, if the provinces so desire, we will be able to repatriate the constitution back to Canada and draft another one which will guarantee equality to all Canadians and, as we have been wishing for generations, to the French Canadians safety and promotion of the French language not only in Quebec but throughout Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ENCOURAGE PROVINCIAL CONSULTATION TO REDRAFT THE CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am greatly tempted to follow the example of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) and to take advantage of this important debate to delight in a useless attack on individuals and to forget the real issue, that is national solidarity and the way to achieve it. I do not intend to yield to temptation.
We owe it to ourselves today as always, in response to the motion moved by my Creditiste colleague,-and precisely on account of the very nature of this motion,-to show maturity, true responsibility, faced with the challenge of national solidarity, and to do so in a tone as airily and as serene as that of the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte).
Mr. Speaker, this Canada of ours, this Canada built by our forefathers whose merits have not always been recognized at the time of their retirement, basically, Canada is wanted by all Canadians from Quebec as well as elsewhere.

I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I welcome this debate. I consider myself privileged to speak on behalf of my leader and my colleagues of the Official Opposition. My travels throughout this great country of ours, undertaken at the request of my colleagues, have enabled me to grasp the true meaning and overwhelming impact of our Canadian indentity. Whether in Vancouver, Montreal, Cranbrook, Madoc, Saint-Hyacinthe, Edmonton, Dunnville, or Hinton, I have sensed the desire and unanimous will of all citizens
November 8, 1973

of this country to join forces in an endeavour to build, rather than to destroy. That is why, Mr. Speaker, I shall prefer a positive approach in the course of this debate.
[ Transla tion]
Certainly I am talking here of our own country and not of the present style given to the federal-provincial relations and not of the way the national unity objective is coloured at the present time.
It is true that this debate must allow us to document as much as possible our critics against this government, but it should also give rise in this House and among the population to proper considerations on the national solidarity theme.
It is advisable to reopen the federal-provincial relations record more especially as we are right after an election in Quebec the results and stakes of which are known. All this is particularly advisable more especially as we are facing today the whole energy issue, in Quebec as well in Alberta, and the wranglings if prolonged unduly could undermine the very foundations of Canadian unity.
First, Mr. Speaker, I deplore, because I fear their consequences, the very style and direction which inspire the present federal government, and sometimes even the Quebec government, in federal-provincial relations and consequently with their legal creations, the municipalities.
The Liberal governments now in office in Ottawa as well as in Quebec City, being deeply divided concerning the objective of a new constitution and therefore without any common direction, tend to fall into piecemeal consultation without any general plan.
This lack of direction leads us into feverish activism. In April 1973, seven separate federal-provincial conferences have been held and, tell me, what results did we get?
The present rate of these conferences is more impressive than the results that they are willing to communicate to us are or are likely to be fruitful.
We must-and this constitutes another important aspect of the problem-denounce the secrecy which, before, during and after, too often surrounds bilateral meetings or even federal-provincial conferences. With the help of the media, let the government therefore function in the open, let it not be afraid of enlightening the population, let it not fear especially to have the media play their part.
I regretted this afternoon, as many other hon. members, that the Prime Minister of Canada, in a change of mood, used certain scornful words about employees, civil servants, and said of them-and I am quoting the Prime Minister of Canada, a man who has championed personal liberties-"do their job very badly when they do not reflect crass ignorance".
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that such a general attack, without any differentiation, any subtle distinction, looks quite like an unfair discrimination towards employees in general. If he had had the guts of giving names, of pointing out at some people in particular, instead of casting all the blame on a whole group of citizens, he would have been much more honest.
Constitution
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, these employees do not deserve to be tried on their motives, or to be convicted without trial. Whenever one is concerned with other people's rights, one does not speak this way.
Mr. Speaker, I understand that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) may have some problems. It is not the fault of the Canada Broadcasting Corporation or the employees who are here, in the gallery or elsewhere, if the Prime Minister is in trouble. It is not the fault of employees if the Prime Minister's prestige is falling. It is not the fault of the CBC if polls prove to be unfavourable to the Prime Minister. It is not the fault of the CBC if his ministers are unable to solve the great problems of this country. It is not the fault of the CBC if the Prime Minister's allies, his left wing, are now reviewing their support. In my opinion, before condemning in an unfair way men and women, we should act with a lucid mind and not give away to panic.
Mr. Speaker, the public is aware of today's problems thanks to the information media. That is why more and more Canadians, in Quebec as elsewhere, are wondering about the nature and form of short term solutions brought to the problems facing our country.
Whether we refer to the hard problem of the rising cost of living, to the humiliating plague of unemployment or event to the record of communications or of energy, too often the elements of the problems are coldly, brutally related to matters of federal and provincial jurisdiction. This is a legitimate and understandable withdrawal or reaction, but out of context because there is no sufficient and objective reference to the national importance of a problem. No consideration is being given to the needs and total priorities of a particular region. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, some ministers over-estimate their strength in Quebec and taking an indecent advantage, as regards Canadian unity, of prejudice in their favour and of an overrated reputation, they allow themselves to become arrogant. It is time to put a stop to this.
In my opinion, by their silence and their slips of the tongue, they unconsciously betray the spirit, if not the letter, of our Constitution, work against Canadian solidarity, and distort the identity of each of the five regions of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, that is why I agree with the spirit, if not with the letter, of the motion before us today. In this House, on September 10, the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) commented on the so-called antiinflationary plan announced on September 4, in the following words:
"-the Minister of Energy himself and the Prime Minister-have given Quebec a half hour's notice of the reversal and change of the federal energy policy, and as far as we know, have not advised at all either Alberta or the other provinces concerned." There was no previous consultation, despite what they may suggest, which indicates not only this government's indifference and disdain for the interest of the provinces, as I have said, but it also indicates that this decision was made, as has become the custom of those gentlemen opposite, off-the-cuff and in an atmosphere of political expediency . . .
But the country ought not to be distracted by this spectacular example of federalism by fiat. We ought to observe the massive, total arrogance but above all we must continue to focus upon the substantive issue.

November 8, 1973
Constitution
How do we, in the official opposition, react once the problem has been defined in order to better meet the challenge of Canadian solidarity? Surely if people may be tempted to say that this federal government takes advantage of crises in this country to usurp provincial jurisdictions, we-and it should be the same for all-want merely a realignment of views of the opposing forces in Canada. The two founding races in this country must become again partners in the pursuit of the same objective. Provincial governments must feel involved in the designing of solutions to national problems.
I am persuaded there is enough room in our system for two levels of government, that could both be active and strong and cooperating loyally and effectively. That concept has been lacking for too long and I believe it is the real basis of federalism.
Let us consider for instance the health field. A few years ago, the Liberal government succeeded in thrusting upon the provinces its views and priorities concerning medical services. And as the costs of these programs have reached prohibitive proportions, the government seems to be seeking an easy way out.
These are programs, the principles and methods of which the government designed itself, programs to which it compelled the provinces to comply with after having spoken highly of their merits, and now, it declares that their value is not proportional to their cost. Moreover, not only does the government acknowledge today to be dissatisfied with those programs, but it has the nerve to try to limit its financial responsibilities while compelling the provinces to meet theirs. As far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, I do not imagine that a provincial government which is aware of its responsibilities towards its electors can accept that. This is the reason why we must seriously consider the possible alternatives. One of those, as the leader of my party said in Montreal on April 15, 1973, would be the following:
The federal government must withdraw from shared cost health programs and it must do it by remitting to provinces a larger part of the tax revenues and obviously ensuring an appropriate equalization in this sharing.
Mr. Speaker, I admit that this is not a perfect solution, but it would be more advisable than what this government intends to do. Moreover, it would be an obvious acknowledgement of the right of the provinces to set up their own priorities in an essential area without any federal interference.
If we should adopt this solution of decentralization, we should, of course, ensure that the advantages of the program are transferable from one province to another.
We should also do what is necessary in a context of equalization in order to stimulate consistency in the quality of present services.
One thing is certain anyway: if the government stays in power, the provinces will lose. They will have to maintain the present standards whereas the federal government will limit its financial contribution. I feel this is absolutely unacceptable.

If we are to offer medical care throughout the country according to specific standards, the co-operation of both levels of government is absolutely necessary.
A Progressive Conservative government would not withdraw from the programs leaving the provinces to their fate and it would insist on having its own version of the national standards complied with.
A Progressive Conservative government would proceed to a real consultation to determine the extent to which the federal government should stay involved. This decision would be taken in a collegial fashion. The time when the decisions were taken unilaterally by Ottawa, the time when this arrogant attitude was displayed-the "take it or leave it" attitude-would be long gone. And inasmuch as the federal government would stay involved, it would pay a full and fair share of those programs.
It is in this collegial spirit that we have advocated during the last electoral campaign, the immediate convening, after our taking office, of a federal-provincial conference on the priorities for tomorrow with a view to determine the most urgent problems, to discuss the short-term and long-term solutions and to determine the guidelines of a national economic strategy.
In brief, we want to take another approach to the whole question of joint programs and federal subsidies. And this new approach would apply to regional development as well as social security. As all my colleagues, I would like to see more flexibility, consultation and co-operation in the relations between both levels of government. We will try as much as possible to let the municipalities, provinces and areas determine their own priorities and assume their own decisions. We will show that the central government can act as a catalyst.

I thank you, Mr. Speaker and I also thank all my colleagues. I will try not to impose upon your kindness.
We will therefore see, Mr. Speaker, that the central government becomes a catalyst of understanding and a factor of unity within confederation.
For the moment, we prefer to stress the urgency of holding a national conference of priorities instead of an early reopening of the Victoria file. It seems to me necessary to move along those lines. The present or future constitution, repatriated or not, is only, with all due
November 8, 1973

respect to the constitutionalists, a kind of instrument to enlighten the government of our country.
First of all, faced with modern problems such as the supply of resources and the quality of the individual and collective life, and facing the future, we must identify the priorities of each partner in our political system, and then, secondly, proceed with the required juridictional and fiscal sharing. Such a process will prepare the minds to a new Victoria, more assured this time of a real success. If other and faster methods to amend the constitution were found, I, for one, would be most interested.
Mr. Speaker, whatever may be the new approach to federal-provincial relations we must, of course, concern ourselves with the question of the official languages in this country, with the easier access for French-speaking people to the federal public service and with federal services provided in both official languages. All that is part and parcel of the national community of interests. However, such a community of interests would be really and fully achieved only to the extent that we find solutions to the economical and social problems in each of the five major areas in this country. The real Canadian challenge consists in being able to reconcile social and economic interests at the regional level and as this motion points out, "to meet the basic aspirations of each province".
And here, Mr. Speaker, I should like to give the following warning: one must not see more than there really is in the last result of the elections in Quebec. If, on the one hand, we must again rejoice at the victory of the federalist philosophy over separatism, on the other hand, one must not forget that the Parti Quebecois increased the number of its supporters to 30 per cent in the vote. And most of all, one must understand that the victory of the federalist option in Quebec does not mean in any way that there are no more problems between Ottawa and Quebec. Let us not bury our head in the sand.
I suggest that as early as the day after October 29, a new chapter of Canadian history opened in Quebec and throughout this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ENCOURAGE PROVINCIAL CONSULTATION TO REDRAFT THE CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I notice that I am the first person to intervene in this debate who is not from the Province of Quebec. I quite understand the reason. This is a subject of very special interest in the Province of Quebec. I hope my intervention is symbolic of the fact that it is also of considerable interest, or, if it is not, it should be, to Canadians from other provinces.
We do not adopt the language of the resolution which has been presented to us, but we do say that the presentation of this resolution performs, in our view, a useful service. It is proper that, from time to time, this House should turn its attention not only to the broad problems of Canadian unity but to the questions arising under our constitution which are unsettled and which require solution in the interest of unity in Canada.
Others in this debate have spoken of the recent election in Quebec. I do not propose to make any political or partisan comments, but 1 think I speak for people who believe in the federal system throughout Canada when I
Constitution
say that we welcomed its result, not from a partisan point of view but because it demonstrated that, at the present time at least, the option for separatism was not being chosen by the people of Quebec. But I should like to underline that this election is no basis for complacency. The constitutional issue is one that cannot be allowed to drift or be allowed to be ignored by the people of Canada; I believe the constitution of Canada needs changes made to it, and needs careful consideration at the present time.
One of the most disappointing parts of my experience in this House was being a member of a committee of which one of the co-chairman was the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan) and comprised of representatives of all parties in this House and the Senate. This committee travelled throughout Canada, listened to innumerable briefs from learned people, and prepared a report which represented a general consensus of people in all regions of Canada. The committee made 104 proposals in its report, yet the government of the day has seen fit, as far as I can make out, completely to ignore that report. It has done nothing about any of the recommendations that were made. Although the report was a weighty one it has disappeared, just as a very weighty rock might disappear into the ocean, without trace. The report caused scarcely a ripple. I consider this disappointing and I hope the situation will be remedied. The report I refer to represented a useful consensus. We did not all agree about everything, but at least we demonstrated that when people of good will from across Canada sit down to tackle problems, they can reach a high level of agreement and arrive at a basis for the renewal of our constitution.
The report contained one proposal that I think we ignore at our peril. The report states that Canada needs a new and modern constitution which would eliminate much of what is obsolete and inadequate in the present British North America Act. I acknowledge that it is well known that constitutional matters sometimes appear technical and difficult, partly because they are often discussed by constitutional lawyers, such as myself, who are somewhat versed in the legal phraseology of the constitution and its ramifications. Nevertheless, it remains true that the basic and fundamental rights of the people of this country rest upon the constitution. The unity of this country rests upon the constitution. The constitution impinges upon the lives of our people at every level, and if we do not have an intelligent, modern, flexible constitution which is capable of dealing with the problems of the country, we will fail to meet the challenges that lie ahead.
One aspect of the constitution in which we in this party are interested, and have been for very many years, is the question of fundamental and basic rights. We think that these should be entrenched in our constitution. We have long argued that this is fundamental to a free society such as Canada's should be. We have been reminded of the importance of this by a recent decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in the Lavell case in which the majority of that court gave a decision which seemed to indicate that our present Bill of Rights passed by this parliament is totally inadequate to protect large sections of this community against discrimination, such as discrimination against sex. There are many women in this country who are demanding, and I say justly demanding, that we entrench a clear-cut protection against discrimination on

November 8, 1973
Constitution
the ground of sex in our constitution. The same applies equally to discrimination on the ground of religion, race or other areas where discrimination is frequent. We want to see these basic freedoms entrenched in the constitution.
There is no better time to set about this. I, and all members of the House, know that for a good many years there has been a series of federal-provincial constitutional conferences which have failed to produce an effective result. One of the reasons for this was that at least four of the provinces in western Canada were represented by governments that can politely be called small "c" conservative. They were opposed to any change in this field and presented an obstacle to proposals such as the entrenchment of the Bill of Rights in the constitution.
As a result of the fortunes of elections, those four governments-I refer to the governments of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba-have been replaced by governments ready to take a more flexible, may I say more basically Canadian, attitude toward this question. The election in Quebec is now out of the way and Quebec seems to have opted for federalism. I do not think it has opted for a status quo federalism; I think it has opted for federalism that is ready to change, to advance and to accommodate itself in light of present circumstances.
Furthermore, we think that the consitution should recognize the special position of the native people of this country. We agree also that actual constitutional changes in this field should await full consultation with organizations of native people when they have completed their present research. This is one aspect with regard to which there are recommendations in the report of the joint committee to which I have referred.
I should like to say a little more about that committee report because I think it deserves much more attention than it has had. The most essential constitutional question in any confederation is the division of powers as between the federal and provincial legislatures. We accept the basic proposal in the report that the powers of the provincial legislature should be enlarged in all areas touching upon social and cultural policy. The powers of the federal parliament should be clarified and enlarged in regard to important economic policies that affect Canada as a whole.
Perhaps this is not the right place to go into them in detail, but the report refers to income support measures. We think this is an ingenious solution to this particular problem. We recognize the fact that at the present time, so far as we understand it, in the field of welfare the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) has been pursuing a course of very close and fruitful collaboration with the various provincial governments. We think that is an excellent thing. It underlines the advisability of solving jurisdictional difficulties at the present time.
There is a subject mentioned in the report in which I am particularly interested, and about which I am concerned. That is the problem of air and water pollution. Once again we run into a field where the constitutional confusion is tremendous. When the British North America Act was written people did not live in the sort of society where air and water pollution were of serious dimension. But we do,

and yet we are hampered in our efforts to clear up our environment and provide a better quality of life by the confusion that exists as to jurisdiction. The report to which I refer recommends that if national standards are to be set there should be an over-all, paramount federal power. It says that the importance of the contribution of the provinces with respect to air and water pollution cannot be denied, but stresses that the overriding and paramount power to clear up pollution, which so often extends beyond provincial boundaries, should be clearly vested in the federal authority.
I do not think it would be helpful at this stage if I were to go into details about other things in this report. Many of them are important to the people of Canada, and the people of Canada will suffer if we neglect to deal with these things when we have the opportunity to do so. I do, however, want to refer to the battle against inflation. In this particular regard we found the report very inadequate. It said:
In cases of national emergency, as defined by the Parliament of Canada, the Provinces should delegate to the Federal Parliament all additional powers necessary to control prices, wages and other forms of income, including rent, dividends and profits, to implement its prime responsibility for full employment and balanced economic growth.
Everybody in this House knows that the question of control of wages, prices and other forms of income, profits and so on, is of vital importance in the battle against inflation. Yet anybody who has taken the trouble to look at the facts will know there is immense confusion as to who it is has jurisdiction to deal with this matter.
I know that the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan) spent much time lecturing and talking to people about some of the confusion that exists. The case books are full of cases dealing with this problem and what emerges is still confusion, so that no one knows who is responsible for dealing with many of these matters. While we do not seek greater centralization of powers, if we are to have an effective battle against inflation we must recognize that where it is necessary to deal with important matters which effect the economy at the national level, then this power should be clarified in the constitution. Who can deny that the inflationary spiral has important economic effects at the national level?
There are other challenges facing Canada at the present time. One of the challenges with which we are all familiar, because we hear so much about it every day and will continue to hear about it for some time into the future, is the energy crisis. We in this party want to make it clear that while we recognize the provinces have interests and concerns in natural resources,-they have the proprietary rights in natural resources-yet when a crisis hits the whole national economy there is a federal responsibility to take action in that field. We support what the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) said the other day, that it is the parliament and government of Canada that must act responsibly in dealing with a situation that affects the well-being of all Canadians, and which of course has implications beyond the boundaries of Canada.
I conclude, therefore, by reiterating that the introduction of this subject by this motion in our opinion is a healthy and worthwhile thing, and I urge the federal
November 8, 1973

government not to waste the opportunity that exists at the present time to deal with and solve some of these problems. The sort of lackadaisical, laissez faire attitude of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), although he is an expert in constitutional affairs, is not good enough. These problems ought to be dealt with. They may be difficult. They may not arouse great popular enthusiasm in some parts of the country, but if they are ignored they may rise to plague us in the future and make government in Canada less helpful to the people than it should be.

But having heard the hon. Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) as well as the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner), I believe this motion comes in the nick of time and shows an objective approach. My colleague did not try to rouse members one against another, he was very constructive when he said that it was about time Canada should give provinces, through a constitution adjusted to needs, a greater autonomy, more facilities for self-determination
Constitution
and to determine by themselves their cultural, economic and political destiny.
Mr. Speaker, my colleague from Champlain did not insult anybody. He stated facts, real situations, things we live through and I was surprized to hear the hon. minister make a clear election speech, in a style that has been outmoded for at least 25 years, a pure and simple political speech. First, he said exactly the opposite of what his leader said on the day following the famous October 29 election in Quebec. He said people had voted Liberal, that the Liberal party was the greatest party.
His leader said, on the evening of election day, that Quebecers had voted for Canada and against separation. Here, Mr. Speaker, I would very much like to make a comparison between separatism and provincial independence. There is one difference. Seceding from a country is not like being part of that country and being oneself, free of all kinds of control. Seceding from a country is completely different from remaining part of it and being oneself.
I think the motion of the hon. member for Champlain is clear and specific enough but, as usual, some people will say that maybe Creditistes are separatists. I believe we have shown in this House that we are Canadians, but we want to be first class Canadians and to be respected throughout Canada.
My colleague suggests in his motion that the provinces should be given more freedom. What are the provinces asking for? We hear in this House spokesmen for the various provinces of Canada. I hear the member for Gan-der-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan) speaking day in and day out about Newfoundland. I am sure that people in Peace River do not know much about Newfoundland, but the people of that province are aware of the situation there. They tell us of their problems, and say: Give us this, or give us that. All the provinces are in the same position. It is the same in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. What do the members of parliament from the west talk about? Of the wheat in Saskatchewan and the oil in Alberta. In Manitoba and Saskatchewan, people talk about agriculture. speechtext:
On top of that, we are consistent with ourselves, we do not try and lie to the people, we tell them exactly what we think.
Mr. Speaker, I said a while ago that the warning issued to the Liberal party, the central government, is a serious one. In 1970 there was trouble caused by the FLQ, by all sorts of organizations which wanted and still want Quebec to withdraw from confederation. They are even prepared to resort to violence and that violence is not totally extinct. The threats of violence are not totally extinct.
Time will tell, there is still time to save the Canadian ship; nobody more than I wishes to remain a Canadian in the full sense of the word, but in my province I would like the government to have more latitude, just as much as I want the same latitude for any other province in Canada, to allow them to make decisions. That is why we ask, even at the risk of becoming the laughing-stock of everybody, that the Bank of Canada be used in the provinces' interests and set branches in all Canadian provinces, for the purpose of serving them and making financially possible what is already physically possible in each of them. Only then would disappear the risk of destruction which looms over the Canadian confederation, because the provinces would be autonomous and free without being separated.
For that matter, Mr. Speaker, all human beings, hon. members included, want to be independent. Everyone dreams about his independence. We do not want anybody to tell us what we have to do. Provinces and even municipal boards want more freedom, as well as school boards. Mr. Speaker, when are we free, when are we a little independent? When we have a purchasing power. Then we have the permission to choose, to refuse, to decide. It is said that money does not create happiness. No, but it helps a little.
November 8, 1973

All provinces complain about a lack of financial resources; even Ontario complainseabout it although it is the richest province in Canada. The province of Quebec lacks financial means. It meets with federal authorities. The latter make us sing all day long the song of the lack of money. Mr. Speaker, independence exists for each and every province and each of them would be much more interested in building up Canada as we want it, namely a united, strong and free Canada. Beside, Canadian independence does exist. We can hear hon. members of the New Democratic Party especially continuously speak against American imperialism, say that we are ruled by the Americans who control our natural resources. That is true! Ottawa does not do anything about it. In the province of Quebec, the Bay James development project is now under way, and who is financing it? The Americans. With what? With American dollars. In wheelbarrows? No. With some figures written down on a promisory note. Why do they not use the Bank of Canada to arrive at figures based on the same wealth that give the value to the monetary system?
Mr. Speaker, during the election, we heard about the famous P.Q. budget, for an amount of $11 billion dollars. When we referred to the guaranteed annual income, it was a real scandal. A television debate was held on Year 1 of separatism and on a budget prepared by Mr. Parizeau, a guy who I think advised two or three premiers of the province of Quebec, and he led the whole gang to defeat because he had no good advice to give. Mr. Speaker, we heard of this project and I already hear the Liberal answer; Your dollar will only be worth 50c. Mr. Loubier says: I think that it will only be worth 30c. They frightened people with that.
What gives money its value? The will of the Prime Minister or the capacity of people to produce in their country or in their province? And what is preventing this? I do not believe in the separatist argument that a Bank of Quebec should be set up, separate from the rest of Canada. Not at all. We produce in Quebec about 30 per cent of what we consume, everybody knows it. However, what is preventing us from using the Bank of Canada to help all provinces, including Quebec? You would then see, during all future federal-provincial or provincial conferences, that no one would complain about the lack of money. They would rather speak of the mutual development of natural resources, which would be much more logical than the stupidities that we are now witnessing during federal-provincial conferences.
Mr. Speaker, American imperialism is not enough. Soviet imperialism is coming. The New Democratic Party does not talk as much about it. That is not known, but it is another kind of imperialism.
When the Soviets impose their administration, their decisions on other countries, including Cuba-at a certain moment it was on Chile, today it is on other countries-we do not hear the NDP protest against it. No, it is normal. It is called the revolution set to save human beings. As for those who oppose it, we are told that they take to repression. Then, the NDP oppose repression and are in favour of revolution. In China, it is the same thing: the Chinese who were all considered as bandits by Canadians ten years ago
Constitution
are now considered as saints in frock coat. What can we do? It works now.
Mr. Speaker, we do not want American imperialism. We want co-operation between countries. We want an independent Canada. We do not want to lose our Canadian identity. In Quebec, we do not want to lose identity as Quebecers either. We don't want the British Columbia people to lose their identity and it is rather amusing to find they don't want to be dictated to by Ontario. The same applies to the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and the Maritimes. Mr. Speaker, those are the provinces that should incite not political speeches like the one delivered by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, but positive action. If we want to save Canada, the time is now, tomorrow will be too late. And it is not in blood that we should do so but through reasoning, the good will to remain free people in a country respected by the whole world.
