subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ENCOURAGE PROVINCIAL CONSULTATION TO REDRAFT THE CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like many members, I had the opportunity to read the motion of the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte). It makes us think a great deal. I find it somewhat surprising that a few days after the Quebec election that took place on October 29, people would criticize that election. They want to challenge the result. They want to say that people were afraid.
I say to this House, as I lived through what went on in Quebec, as I was involved in the election campaign, that Quebecers are not timid people. If the Creditistes want us to believe in this House that Quebecers are fearful people, I say it is the opposite. Quebecers have common sense. They were offered certain very clear political options, some others that were indistinct and others thouroughly nebulous. The Liberal party said: What did Mr. Bourassa's team offer during all that election campaign? Profitable federalism. He showed throughout Quebec what profitable federalism meant. Figures were given in support of that. They did not present a Year 1 budget in which a good deal of things were forgotten. A billion dollars was forgotten and they did not know how to get it back. One can recall the television debate, where Mr. Parizeau tried to defend his budget.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, what was offered to the Quebec people? Physical security. As the hon. member for Champlain said a while ago: What do people look for in a system? They look for physical security. I should like to add that they also look for social security. They also seek political security. But they seek above all-and that is what the Quebec Liberal party and their leader Mr. Bou-rassa offered the Quebec people-order and justice.
Referring to the October events, we saw a minister of justice who asserted himself, who assumed his responsibilities and who restored order in Quebec.
Another thing, Mr. Speaker, in connection with the first-year budget of the Parti Quebecois. The federal government was blamed during the entire electoral campaign for having imposed the war measures.
In the "National expenses" item, mention is made that in an independent Quebec, 8,000 soldiers would be maintained. Why 8,000 soldiers? Merely to protect our territory. To my knowledge, Canada has been existing for 100 years,

November 8, 1973
Constitution
and there has never been any militia to protect Canada from the United States. But we were strong and respected. Why do Messrs. Levesque and Parizeau not tell Canadians that once they are separated, invasion will come?
Second, why a militia of 8,000 men? Simply, they answer, in order to meet a few cases of national emergency. Well, in October 1970, we had a case of national emergency. They themselves even provide for votes to that effect in their own budget.
So, Mr. Speaker, we see what the Parti Quebecois has to offer. But what can Social Credit offer us? At a certain time, it favours independence or supports an independen-tist government, but subject to the condition that they change the monetary system. They also suggest a plebiscite, but I think that the best one that we could have has been given by the people of Quebec last October 29, by saying "no" to the PQ, separation, independence and yes to a profitable federalism.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, even though Mr. Bourassa was reelected premier of Quebec with 102 seats, there are still going to be problems in the province of Quebec. During the last provincial campaign, the Parti Quebecois tried to persuade us of the contrary, suggesting that once independence is achieved, there would be no problems any more in the province of Quebec.
No intellectually honest man would dare make such a statement. As I have stated on many occasions during the provincial elections, I feel that even with a very strong Liberal government, there will still be squabbles with the federal government. What is federalism? It is a dialogue. But before a dialogue can take place, there must be problems. The Trudeau, Pearson and St-Laurent administrations have caused problems over the years because they even refused to dialogue with the provinces to help them solve the problems confronting Quebec and the rest of Canada. But if they still want to speculate on the voting result of October 29 last, I think this is not honest. That vote was not one for the past but for youth, for the future and to enable us to keep on growing freely within all the scope of the word "free". I would certainly put into question the coming into power of a Pequiste government in Quebec because we would then cease to be free.
But we are really living this freedom and, in my opinion, as a Canadian, as a Quebecer I am going on living it. If we compare the economic point of view of federalism with that of separatism what was done during that election campaign, what have the Pequistes done?
They went across the province of Quebec with their Year One budget. They forgot so many facts that they were forced to plan little regional programs. They have established one for my own area. But they forgot merchant marine, the assistance to shipbuilding, and they forgot also the question of a direct link which will cost between $200 and $300 million, and the merchant marine, about $1 billion.
They forgot that in our region. Those people were in such deep trouble by the end of the election campaign that they had even thought of the Progressive Conservative party for Quebec, during the last campaign. Mr. Wagner himself, the member for Saint-Hyacinthe, came in our area
[Mr. Guay (Levis)J
and told us: If I forgot to promise you anything, to tell you something, I promise you anyway.
That is not the way to act in politics, Mr. Speaker, but we must be honest, and the Liberal party in Quebec made really honest and sensible proposals to the Quebec people, and they gave it an answer.
In conclusion, I would like to quote an article on the economy. This quotation is from Le Soleil, April 7, 1964: What do economists think of separatism?
Even in the most favorable circumstances, they generally agree that it would bring about a decrease in our standing of living. Thus, an economist like Andre Raynauld, director of the Economic Science Department at the University of Montreal thinks that the standard of living in Quebec, which is presently 28 per cent lower than that of Ontario, would fall to 50 per cent for an indefinite period.
On the other hand, Gerard Filion who is not properly speaking an economist but who is actively involved in the present economic life of Quebec as director of the General Investment Corporation, said two weeks ago in Rimouski that the major obstacle to the separation of Quebec is the decrease in the standard of living. According to him, separation would cause secondary industry to slow down considerably. Referring to two cases of immediate concern to him, the director of this public organization pointed out that the Forano and the Volcano industries, taken over by the G.I.C., would see their turnover reduced by half if Quebec separated. He also gave the example of the Quebec furniture market, 30 per cent of which is aimed at the Canadian market, which would be severely affected. At the same time, the director of the G.I.C. said that with its steel industry, the province of Quebec would exceed the economic prosperity of Ontario. This is probably nothing more than an unproved statement. Yet it was made by someone who is intimately involved in the every day realities of the Quebec economy.
I should like also to mention the editorial of Claude Ryan in Le Devoir of Friday, October 26, 1973. This editorial which is entitled "The Choice of October 29, Today's Option" reads as follows:
The tendency today is towards the establishment of larger social, economic, and even political entities. To abandon the kind of experience that is Canada, it would require imperious and urgent reasons. These reasons cannot be found as yet in Quebec, at least they have not reached a level or a degree capable of gaining approval.
Canadian federalism has been often criticized. There was reason to deplore its difficult adaptation to the Quebec situation, but one should not hasten to infer from that that it is no longer possible for the Quebec community to develop within the federal system.
He concludes his editorial by referring to the silent majority, and I quote:
-they prefer for the time being that Quebec keeps on seeking its way in Canadian federalism. This preference is the result of some sound realism. We shall see tomorrow how it will express itself through Monday's voting.
Well, this vote was definitely confirmed before the population of all the provinces of Canada-because they were concerned-and before all the premiers. They were all wondering about the result of the vote and, as I said earlier, the people in Quebec answered: We vote not for an adventure, not for some vague promise, but for a realistic system. This is my opinion, Mr. Speaker, and I will keep on defending it in this House.
November 8, 1973

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not going to speak about the Quebec election, except in one sense. However, we have had an interesting afternoon hearing about it. I will just refer in two sentences to the speech of the hon. member for Temis-camingue (Mr. Caouette). I wondered if within the ranks of the Social Credit Party there were those who were classified by any of the rest of my colleagues as being separatists.
I do not want to be pretentious when I say this, but my colleagues and I have had reason to doubt the thrust of the Social Credit Party. However, we have had no reason to doubt their loyalty to this country. I would have thought that separatism would have been the last adjective they would use, including the hon. member for Temiscamingue. He mentioned the futile search some years ago in the halls of Westminster for the constitution of Canada. That was a light-hearted reference. The document, of course, is there in the statutes.
It is not a bad idea to remind ourselves it is an acute embarrassment to our colleagues in the British parliament, and successive British governments, that we in Canada have not yet been able to make the constitutional arrangements so that we can patriate the constitution and find an amending formula that is acceptable. I might say in passing that surely there are many things we want to charge the British government with from time to time, but we could never mount a successful argument that it is they who are resisting the wish to patriate the constitution. When some of our colleagues from European parliaments were here last week, a British member of parliament, Mr. Kirk, said to me, for Heaven's sake when are you people going to find a way to get the document or statute back to Canada? I did not have time to wander through 105 years history, but after a little time we perhaps understood each other better on this issue.
A wise and distinguished Canadian, Robertson Davies, said recently that Canadians are suffering from linguistic inflation. I want it to be clearly understood that has nothing to do with the official languages. Although I wish my facility in French were better, I suspect that Robertson Davies charge would also apply to the French language. If so, I grieve for them. However, he was referring to the English language and the fact that nowadays a good many people lard or load their language with slogans, adjectives and adverbs and in a way have expectations of people about governments almost impossible to fulfil.
I hope the cabinet will not think I have gone soft on them or anything, but I am struck by the fact that almost any government of almost any political stripe is having a difficult time today in fulfilling the expectations of people. I suspect one of the reasons is that many of us, and I suppose we should all say, "mea culpa" or take the blame, are guilty of linguistic inflation. Robertson Davies went on to say:
Language in Canada today is being broken down and rubbed away by people who care nothing for words . .. They have debased the coinage of language to the point where we have a dangerous condition of linguistic inflation in which thought is clouded and feeling degraded.
Constitution
I just make the plea, without discussing the arrangement of constitution-making, that we should try not to be trapped by Robertson Davies' phrase "linguistic inflation". It is a difficult subject that is almost trite to us.
The notice of motion, I say with great respect to the mover, is in a way an example of linguistic inflation. Despite what one's views may be about constitutional evolution in Canada, I do not think reform is helped by the extravagant wording of the motion. My party believes the stars are now in the right position to begin again the consulting process in preparation for the day we all look forward to, the day that we patriate the constitution with an amending formula flexible enough to meet the demands of the future of all the country and yet sufficiently sensitive so as to give no cause for alarm to any of the groups of peoples who make up this country.
When talking about this motion, as far as I am concerned, it would be quite wrong for me to attempt an analysis of the results of the Quebec election and the mandate given to the Liberal government there. All I want to say is that surely it is not an overstatement to state that the premier and government can now speak with the authority that 102 seats gives them in the National Assembly. I am not discussing whether 102 seats is a good or a bad thing. That is for others to discuss or we might discuss it on another occasion. All I am saying is that nobody can say the premier or government of Quebec approaches constitutional amendment with lack of confidence from the people. I think this is a significant change.
I am going to try a paradox because I believe it is not such a bad thing in 1973 that the government of Canada faces constitutional evolution in a minority position. I suspect this situation should be a bit chastening to a government, one which will demand less of what I might call confrontation politics and more consultation politics. It is another paradox about our country that we seem to enjoy an international reputation as peacemakers. Although there is some difficulty about the arrangements, they really are not the fault of Canada. However, we seem to have a terrible time trying to arrange our affairs domestically in a suitable manner.
I am troubled by those who see the future of this country decided by simple slogans like "One Canada". "One Canada" is a copout by people who really do not want to think of the constitutional arrangements. Then, there are those, and I regret to say it, who glory in our divisions. They surely are the traitors in our times. There are also those who pander to bigots. All I can say is that the cup from which they drink contains poison.
I was glad to hear the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) mention the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on the Constitution. I do not have very much time, but I want to reflect on one or two of the recommendations. I very much hope that some of the recommendations the members of the committee were able to make will not only be useful, and that is not a strong enough word, but will be incorporated in the new constitution of Canada. I have taken the time to underline a couple of them. For instance, recommendation No. 2 reads:
A new Canadian constitution should be based on functional con-
November8, 1973

Constitution
siderations which would lead to greater decentralization of governmental powers in all areas touching culture and social policy and to greater centralization of powers which have important economic effects at the national level. Functional considerations also require greater decentralization in many areas of governmental administration.
Unfortunately for the country, I have never tried to bore the House with fiscal or monetary theories. I am not informed on this subject. But perhaps the fact that I am not makes it possible for me to say this: I have never understood how a federal government, the national government of the country, could possibly execute useful fiscal and monetary policies when ten provincial governments and many of their agencies, and large agencies at that-I think of Quebec Hydro, Ontario Hydro and others-are able to go to the financial marketplaces of the world without even a bow in the direction of the federal government and make arrangements which obviously could have adverse effects on national policy. This is the kind of thing which recommendation No. 2 would, I hope, seek to prevent.
Then we come to the recommendation about our native peoples. Here we find another of the paradoxes of Canada because we, that is, all of us in our representative capacity, are on a collision course. What we are dealing with is question involving two basic rights, rights which as far as I can see cannot be reconciled at this stage in history. I am thinking now of the Bedard and Lavell case before the Supreme Court of Canada. I do not wish to bore the House by attempting an analysis of the judgment in that case. The problem is that the legitimate aspirations of the women of Canada to have their status at least delineated and dealt with in an entrenched declaration of human rights, or an entrenched bill of rights, is in collision with a recommendation we have made that no constitutional changes affecting native people should be made until such time as their own organizations have completed their research into questions of treaty and aboriginal rights in Canada.
We are all getting a good deal of mail on this subject- letters containing legitimate complaints that we are not moving quickly enough as a government or as a parliament in this field of human rights. Yet the dilemma arises directly when we consider the entrenchment of those rights before our native people have had time to advise the government and the parliament as to the nature of their aspirations. I am raising this matter because, as one interested in this conflict, I do not see how the two ministers concerned can resolve it. Both sides are right. Madame Bedard and Madame Lavell are right. Of course they are right. But the native people of Canada are right as well. While looking to the two ministers to reconcile these points of view, it will do us no harm to raise the issue and talk about it dispassionately.
The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) mentioned the recommendation of the special committee on regional disparities. We were not able to put into a fundamental form the rights of people in certain parts of Canada to enjoy equality of opportunity, and so on, but this should not confuse or discourage people. The difficulty we faced was this: we did not feel it was responsible to give citizens a right of action against the government because they might not enjoy each and every right, in the

economic sense, that their neighbours enjoyed. But I am certain it is equally important in our thinking about constitution-making that men and women taking home pay cheques 40 per cent below those which people in provinces such as Ontario and British Columbia are receiving-60 cents as compared with a dollar-have rights in the economic field just as strong as those of our citizens who properly and wisely treasure their linguistic and cultural inheritance.
There are many other points made in the report of the special committee. There were, in fact, more than 100 recommendations. I, too, welcome this debate because it gives us a chance to take out the report which was tabled in 1972, dust it off if need be, and remind parliament that within its covers are a good many recommendations which if adopted would have a positive effect upon federal arrangements.
Lastly, I would refer hon. members to an interesting statement in an editorial in the August issue of the Journal of Canadian Studies. The article was discussing a review which Mr. Claude Ryan made of some of the writings of Andre Laurendeau. I shall not bore the House with the whole thing, but if I read the editorial describing the review correctly, the point is that it is no longer right or legitimate or fair-here I am chiding English Canadians, so I am on safe ground, I hope-for English Canadians to carry on defining their culture, as the editorial says, in terms of biculturalism, as has been fashionable in certain circles of English Canada, as an excuse for English Canada failing to develop a culture of its own.
Anyone who has listened to the ongoing Canadian debate during the last decade has heard this sort of talk- "We need this special relationship with our French-speaking brothers and sisters because it is the way in which we can be different from the Americans." I think this demeans both sides of this partnership. It is no longer fair and sensible for English Canadians to "cop out" on their side from a federal arrangement which all of us should consider as a very special and treasured possession.
[ Translation]

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the only solution put forward by the federal government to the constitutional problem resides in the Victoria charter, this lure for the province of Quebec, which is besides rejected by all the people of Quebec.
The last provincial election in Quebec, which took place on October 29, places us in front of a clear and precise fact, an unequivocal situation and it places the rest of Canada in front of a hard fact: one person out of three in Quebec wants the independence of the province and the proportion goes up to 35 per cent when we consider only the vote of French Canadians.
In the face of such a situation, Canada does not have the leisure to look arrogantly at what happens in the province of Quebec. Canada must have a firm attitude and show all possible objectivity during the coming months. It must not poke up the fire nor provoke violence by reiterating its excessively arrogant and provocative positions. The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) must not forget that
November 8, 1973

Her Majesty Elizabeth II is still the Queen of Canada and that he is not on the throne.
If it claims to have reached maturity, Canada cannot shut its eyes on the problems which are raised and understood by a very large portion of Quebec. The issue in Quebec is much more a constitutional problem than one of independence.
I say very coolly that there are a lot more independen-tists and separatists without the province of Quebec than there are within. I consider that the attitude of Englishspeaking Canadians towards French-speaking Canadians is much more separatist than that of Quebecers militating within the Parti Quebecois. When one sees that French Canadians with equal qualifications earn less then English Canadians, that bilingual French Canadians with equal-and sometimes higher qualifications because they are bilingual-earn less than English Canadians, then I ask, who are the separatists in Canada?
All political parties in the province of Quebec strongly advocated a constitutional reform, and even the Quebec Liberal party-probably to build up political capital- because how can you want the provincial Liberal Party, which is continuously towed by the federal Liberal Party, to have any concern for the French-Canadian nation when its line of thoughts and action are dictated by Mother Superior in Ottawa?
That has always been its main concern no matter what the situation people faced and are still facing. All political parties in Quebec as the federal Liberal Party, the Progressive Conservative Party and the New Democratic Party demanded on several occasions in the last several years a constitutional revision to allow the province of Quebec to fulfill itself in an environment of peace and prosperity. The federal government would always find a clever and hypocritical way of holding back and extending that situation from one federal-provincial conference to another. The federal government has always managed to create hopes and illusions.
The time has come to take our responsibilities and allow the provinces to take theirs. And since confederation was created by the provinces it is up to them to review it.
When in 1864, and finally in 1867, the Fathers of Confederation agreed to create a confederate system so as to meet more adequately the needs of each province they did not need a centralist federal government such as the current one to reach an agreement.
Since the advent of confederation 106 years have gone by; the needs have changed, the country has become bigger, additional provinces have joined to enrich it with their participation. But today's needs are not those of 1867. Each Canadian province has different needs which are often difficult to understand from one province to the other. We note regretfully that British Columbia finds it hard to understand the Newfoundland attitude as does Prince Edward Island with Manitoba or Alberta.
It is well-known that the French-Canadian nation does not understand confederation and federal government as the other provinces do. They do not have the same feelings because the other provinces have progressively been led to believe that the only important, powerful and reliable government is the federal government.
Constitution
This is understandable since the federal government has always been composed of a majority of English-speaking people and mainly administered by English-speaking people. Outside Quebec the French-speaking reality does not exist.
If you visit western Canada and linguistic problems and bilingualism are brought up, the Ukrainian will say that for him the first language is English and the second, Ukrainian) the German will say that English is the first language and German the second, and the Polish will also tell you that English is the first language and Polish the second. If you try to make them believe the second official language of Canada is French, they will be stunned and will take you for some lunatic or day dreamer.
Mr. Speaker, in 1867 the provinces united to create out of nothing a confederal state. And their discussions resulted in a federal government. The federal government was created by the provinces.
Unfortunately, today we are often witnessing an inversion of values within a family, and now children are dictating the behaviour to their parents. Children determine premises in all discussions with their parents; the federal government thrusts its views on the provinces, the federal government dictates work methods to the provinces as if it had created them and they belonged to it.
It is not unusual for the federal government to interfere with the provinces through constitutional conferences. If the provinces got together in 1867 to create the federal government, they do not need it to amend it according their needs. The provinces must dictate to the federal government what they want to get from it. Unfortunately, because of current practices, we are witnessing a conflict between the federal government and the provinces. We find that the baby is now a teenager, but it has not come yet to maturity, and that perhaps it will never achieve it.
The right hon. Prime Minister himself (Mr. Trudeau) said this at the Victoria Conference, and I quote:
Our presence here also shows that the work so boldly started in the Atlantic city of Charlottetown in 1864 is still unfinished.
And it is the right hon. Prime Minister who says that the discussions on Confederation started in 1864 are still unfinished. I think the Prime Minister should wait until those discussions are over before poking his nose where he should not. At this Victoria Conference, the Prime Minister also said, and I quote:
The other English colonies who proclaimed their independence much later learned from our experience; they took their place in the world as full-fledged nations able to implement and amend, if they wished, their own constitution.
Now, Mr. Speaker, when a country is unable to amend its own constitution, it is because it is not a sovereign country but a colony. Mr. Speaker, if we want to be independent on the international level, no longer depend on the British Empire to draw up our own policies, we do not need to review our constitution but rather to draw up a constitution after agreeing with the provinces. What we need is not to amend a constitution that nobody wants, but to bring together the premiers of all provinces, in order to create a federal state that will give satisfaction to all the constituent elements.

November 8, 1973
Constitution
What we need is a constitution where there will be no mention of the word province, but rather of the word state, where our political independence will be proclaimed. It must be noted that if people talk about independence in the province of Quebec, on the political level, Canada still does not have her independence. One only has to see, at the opening of each session, the representative of the Queen of England authorizing us to speak to know that Canada's independence does not exist. And if one of the ten constituent provinces of Confederation talks about political independence, that province is certainly not to be blamed for its initiative and it is certainly not us, in the federal Parliament, who have to teach it a lesson.
Mr. Speaker, the provinces, except Quebec, do not care much about the constitution. At the Victoria Conference, for instance, the Premier of British Columbia was heard to state, and I quote:

the provision of jobs is the most urgent need confronting this Conference and the nation today. The preservation of our natural environment and pollution control are also matters of high priority, and particularly important is the provision of a healthy moral environment in which our young people can grow to maturity.
He also stated that the constitution was not the priority problem that our country had to face and that if such was the situation in February 1968 when the constitutional review was undertaken, this was no more so than in June 1971, in view of the economic recession and rise in unemployment over that relatively short period.
As for the Premier of Nova Scotia, he deals with constitutional review in so far as offshore mining rights are concerned. Obviously, he is not interested in the linguistic problem since, outside Quebec, there is no language problem because everything is done in English.
Mr. Speaker, at the Victoria conference, the Prime Minister of Canada assumed the chairmanship of the conference. The proposal of the federal government was, in my opinion, a fantastic deceit and trickery on Quebec.
Fortunately, the people read his hand and the province of Quebec did not pass under the yolk. Indeed, at the present time, without any amendment to the constitution, Quebec can withdraw any time from confederation, while according to the shrewd proposals of the Prime Minister, Quebec could not dissociate itself from the Confederation Act.
When we read the Victoria agreement, we realize that to amend the constitution, the majority must include in the first place each province whose population before the passage of that proclamation, according to any general census at least 25 per cent of the Canadian people, which means Quebec and Ontario.
The majority must also include at least two of the Atlantic provinces, at least two western provinces, provided the consenting provinces represent jointly, following the last general census preceeding the adoption of this proclamation, at least 50 per cent of the population of all western provinces.
This means that Ontario is in a position to veto any modification requested by Quebec and that British Columbia can also do the same; this is the stumbling block.

If you refer to article 20 of that same Victoria charter, you will find precisely what Canada is made of. You can read that Canada consists of ten provinces, one of which being Quebec, in addition to the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, which means that if Quebec ever decides to leave confederation, it would need-which is not necessary today-to amend article 20, the agreement of a minimum of six provinces including Ontario or of a minimum of seven provinces if British Columbia disagreed. Therefore, this means that Quebec can now leave confederation and, with the Victoria charter, it would be caught in it.
How is it possible for previously independent States to give up their independence for a mess of pottage. What do the other provinces put in the balance? Mr. Speaker, since there are only two minutes left, I would like to inform you that it is six o'clock.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of this debate we heard an impassioned plea for a non-partisan approach to constitutional reform from the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte) who, I regret to say, is not in the House at the moment. However, the words both of the motion he moved and of his speech belied his stated intention. I am willing to give the hon. member the benefit of the doubt with respect to his inten-
November 8, 1973

tions. His intentions may have been in the clouds of objectivity, but his feet remained mired in the mud of partisanship.
I think it is no exaggeration to say that the hon. member has cheapened the whole constitutional debate by accusing the Canadian government of maintaining unity through fear, autocracy and oligarchy. It is not the Government of Canada which has created the problem of separatism and the fear of separatism; it is the activity of a political party in the province of Quebec which has dedicated itself to the destruction of this country. I would like to hear the hon. member denounce them with the same fervour with which he has attacked the Government of Canada this afternoon.
I am ashamed to have to say that this hon. member not only did not denounce separatism, but said he would support it if along with it there would be a Social Credit government. I was ashamed, as a member of this House, to hear this statement. Not only was it offensive to members of this House; it was also highly irrelevant to the political debate.
We all know, including the hon. member, that the inhabitants of a province are free to vote as they wish. The Social Credit party has even succeeded in gaining office in one of the provinces of Canada. The Social Credit party does not need independence to come to power and, as the hon. member well knows, the independence which the separatist party in Quebec promises would not bring the Social Credit party to power. I was especially embarrassed at that moment for the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette), the leader of the party, who has gone across this whole country and taken a stand highly in favour of our country.

speechtext:
That hon. member proclaimed his devotion to Canada again in his speech this afternoon. He need not have done so, because no one in the House is unaware of the fact that he is an ardent federalist. But obviously he was embarrassed by the words of his colleague because he spent his whole speech trying to reinterpret what the hon. member for Champlain had said. Skilful debater that he is, he changed the whole context of the notion of independence to try to show that individual freedom and independence of action by provinces are possible and even necessary within a federal structure. He spoke of independence within a truly united Canada. We would all agree with that, of course, Mr. Speaker. He made his point well.
Obviously, there are independent fields of action provided to the provinces even now by section 92 of the British North America Act. It was not this relative kind of independence that the hon. member for Champlain had in mind, but this was undoubtedly the best recovery possible which his leader could make, in the circumstances, after the hon. member's fumble.
The hon. member for Temiscamingue would also have been disturbed if he had been here to hear the remarks of the hon. member for Drummond (Mr. Boisvert). Admittedly, that hon. member did a good job of refuting one of the points of his colleague, the hon. member for Champlain, who had said in his motion that the federal government
Constitution
had failed to do anything to encourage the provinces to get together in order to amend or redraft the Canadian Constitution. The hon. member for Drummond argued that the federal government had no role at all in constitutional reform and therefore, of course, had no business in trying to provide leadership. The provinces, he said, are states which can leave the country at will, at any time and, as befits such entities, it is their prerogative to set the pace of such negotiations and tell the federal government what they want.
The hon. member for Drummond went on to attack the formula for constitutional amendment agreed on at Victoria, on the ground that it would limit Quebec in a way that it is not presently limited; that whereas now it has the unilateral right to secede from this country if it should so wish, it would lose this right if the Victoria accord came into effect. There are many of us who have criticisms of the amending formula which was agreed to at Victoria. I, personally, would hope that with a more sober government in British Columbia, even that province would not wish to press the excessive claims which it had embodied in the earlier version of the formula, and that it would now be possible to reach a formula in which the role and the position of the western provinces was the same as that of the Atlantic provinces and in which the requirement for agreement was merely for any two provinces, without putting in the protective clause for British Columbia.
But the attack of the hon. member for Drummond on the formula was based on what I might call a "funny" constitutional theory which really has no basis in reality at all. In fact, the law is that the reform of our constitution or any changes have to be made by the British Parliament on an address by both Houses of the Canadian Parliament. That is very well known, Mr. Speaker, and it hardly needs repetition in this place. There is really no role legally for any province in constitutional amendments.
The practice which has tended to evolve is that the provinces be consulted, one might say, by indulgence of the federal government. It may be that at some time the federal government will want to depart from that practice; for example, if it is not possible to get agreement from the provinces in any other way, or if one province should be especially obstinate about agreeing on a new constitutional practice. For the moment, however, the practice is that all provinces are consulted and there is nothing which would allow a single province, Quebec or any other, to have a unilateral right to do what it wishes. However, I hope our solidarity with the people of Quebec does not rest on constitutional formulas but, rather, on a shared past and a shared future.
In the circumstances, perhaps we should be tolerant of the hon. members to our right. I suspect that what we are encountering from that party in this debate is really sour grapes as a result of the Quebec election. I believe it is worth pausing for a moment to reflect on that election and the results of it from the viewpoint of our theory of representation. Even some ardent federalists have been calling the results excessive and not representative of the views of the Quebec people. We hear talk of proportional representation being a better system.

November 8, 1973
Constitution
Of course, the form of voting which the people of Quebec wish to use is for them to decide, but since the theory is also common to this House I hope I may be permitted to say that the theory of representation on which this House proceeds is that our people live in communities and that these communities deserve representation. They deserve the constant type of representation which they get from having a single member of parliament who will speak for their interests and will represent them in their ordinary problems as well as in the great matters of state. This, of course, is not possible under proportional representation.
The Quebec election showed us that in every part of Quebec and indeed in almost every community in that province the people stood for Canada, and not separation from Canada. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this is a very important point for them to have established and it is indeed a true reflection of what the people of Quebec feel and want.
The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) made the point in his remarks that the government has seen fit to ignore the recommendations of the Special Committee on the Constitution of Canada, of which that hon. gentleman was a member and I had the honour to be chairman from this House. In general, I find myself in considerable sympathy with his position and even with many of his remarks today, but I do not believe I can allow to pass his view that the government has seen fit to ignore the recommendations of that committee. That is not what has happened at all. Let us look at some examples.
The bilingualism policy is possibly not the best example because it has other sources as well, but the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) has been proceeding with a bilingualism policy which is in accord with the recommendations of the special committee. In the area of mul-ticulturalism, the policy put forward by the government and which is being administered by the Minister of State responsible for multiculturalism (Mr. Haidasz) is entirely the policy which was recommended by that committee. It is true that in this case the government's policy was announced first, but only after the committee had held extensive hearings across the country at which these views had been presented and at which members of the committee had made their views known, and only after our recommendations had been prepared and imparted to the party caucuses. At that stage, our recommendations were common currency and I think we can feel that the government policy which was adopted before the final recommendation was a reflection of those recommendations.
Perhaps in no area has there been so much implementation of recommendations as in the area of housing. The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) has instituted trilevel conferences, and has generally encouraged greater consultation at the municipal level. As far as the larger cities in the country are concerned, the federal government has been endeavouring to set up permanent trilevel bodies for consultation. The neighbourhood rehabilitation program is full of consultation procedures with the provinces and the local neighbourhoods.
In his budget last spring, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) presented a broader equalization formula which

for the first time would include what happened at the municipal level: a tax base including the municipal level in the equalization formula is something which the committee was urging.
The broadcasting policy which the government put forward, while not one which is entirely acceptable to the provinces at the present time, is one which reflects greater sharing by the provinces, and it was advocated by the special joint committee. Perhaps, above all, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), whom I am pleased to see in the House, has been following one of the most important recommendations of the committee, that of allowing the provinces to share in the mechanism by which family allowances are granted.

You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that the committee recommended that this should be the pattern established by the constitution for demographic grants in general. The minister has been blazing this new trail in his negotiations with the provinces in regard to family allowances. The legislation which is in the process of receiving final approval from the House will allow the provinces to vary the amount paid, so that while a certain minimum payment must be made across the country, a province will be able to vary, according to certain criteria, the amount of money which it pays to its citizens. A province can therefore have a population policy which is based on the feelings of the people in that particular province.
Far from being ignored, Mr. Speaker, the recommendations of the special joint committee are the everyday stuff of federal policy. At the federal level, we might say that this has been one of the most implemented reports in Canadian history. Naturally, the federal government cannot change the constitution on its own; so if this is where one is looking for implementation, it obviously has not yet been possible to do it at this level.
I do not need to detail for members of this House the reasons for the delay, but obviously the federal government has not been responsible for the breakdown of the Victoria negotiations or the constitutional impasse which followed. The federal government has remained constantly open to further negotiations with the provinces. Several times the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has urged the province of Quebec to present new proposals since it was the province primarily responsible for the failure to gain unanimous acceptance of the earlier proposals.
I agree with the hon. member for Greenwood and the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) on the necessity of proceeding with these constitutional negotiations as quickly as possible, but obviously this is not something which is subject to the control of this House or even subject to the control of the federal government. It depends upon the broader political winds in the country. We can here express our hope and desire that these negotiations should take place as soon as possible, that they should be as full as possible and that the federal government should provide the kind of leadership which the report of the special joint committee suggested.
I think it is important to note, lest we get a false emphasis, that constitutional reform is not a one-way street. The special joint committee, it is true, put greater
November 8, 1973

stress on decentralization and especially on what we call the cultural imperative for Quebec. I would read to hon. members a few sentences from the committee report as follows:
We acknowledge a cultural imperative for Quebec; it must have sufficient control over its collective life to ensure the preservation and development of French Canadian culture. Put another way, the constitution must guarantee the preservation of the collective personality of French Quebec. In the expansion of provincial powers which we propose, Quebec would gain new powers to achieve these ends.
That was one of the most important objectives of the committee's work, Mr. Speaker. I believe the primary thrust of the committee's recommendation was one of decentralization. We also point out in our report that there must be changes the other way, that the provinces must also allow the federal government greater latitude. This is important in economic areas. The hon. member for Greenwood spoke about these things this afternoon. I agree with the points he made and there is no need to emphasize them further.
In order to present a balanced point of view, I wish to read some further words of the committee's report as follows:
We have spoken of the need for an increase in both centralization and decentralization, depending on functional considerations. In our view greater decentralization in areas of culture and social policy would benefit all the provinces ...
On the other hand, greater centralization is necessary in the regulation of the economy.
I hope the time for constitutional reform is at hand. I know the federal government is prepared to lead the way. If I may express my personal hope, it is that the federal government will attempt to consummate these changes in one single package deal. I have always felt, personally, that we are more likely to arrive at a satisfactory result if, instead of bartering on a power-by-power basis and trying to do a few things, we sit down, on the basis of the Victoria charter, to do all the work at once so that there can be complete bargaining and a complete exchange of views and concessions from one side to the other. In other words, this exchange should not be a one-way exchange but should be a two-way exchange, as the committee suggested. It seems to me that this would be the most fruitful way for us to work on constitutional reform at present.
However it is done, I know that members of this House will want to express to the government their feelings, and I think they will say that it is time for our constitution to be reformed or to be revised. It should be changed in such a way that the people of Canada will be able to feel that the constitution responds to their needs of the moment and that they can feel more truly Canadian than has been the case under existing mechanisms.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ENCOURAGE PROVINCIAL CONSULTATION TO REDRAFT THE CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to applaud the initiative of the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte) in introducing the motion we are debating. Many members who have spoken before me in this debate have made specific reference to constitutional discussions which have been before us and which have been of concern for some time. I do not intend to repeat what
Constitution
they said or to speak particularly about the direct method of repatriation in a discussing the constitution. I want, instead, to turn my attention tonight and the attention of the House to that atmosphere of co-operation which is necessary before there can be an amendment of the constitution and which is necessary, indeed, before the constitution can be made to work.
I was interested in hearing the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) indicate this afternoon that a debate on this topic is usually a debate which is of special interest to members of this House from the province of Quebec, because in that province there is a special interest in constitutional matters. Sir, it used to be that members of this House from Alberta were able to more or less take a spectator's seat in those discussions on federal-provincial relations. That is not the case tonight.
It is natural that I should view and enter this debate against the context of the current deep dispute about energy matters between Alberta and Ottawa. No Albertan could escape that context because, sir, there is an anger in Alberta now that exceeds in intensity anything in my memory or in the memory of older men than I. It is not anger that other people would want to use our oil, our resources. We want them to. Moreover, we want Canadian consumers to have a better price and better access to our resources than nationals of other countries. The Premier of Alberta has made that clear. Instead, sir, the anger in Alberta is about the methods this government has used to implement a policy which, while it is important to every region of Canada, is most important to Alberta because it affects not only our price of fuel and our prospects of warmth but our capacity to grow and to industrialize.
This is not the place to debate the merits of particular federal proposals regarding energy. Those have been debated on other occasions in this House, and will be again. The debate inspired by this motion concerns, not the merits of a particular case but the methods by which our federal system works. In many ways, this is the most appropriate forum for a review of the Alberta situation, because whatever disagreement might exist about the merits of the actions proposed by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald), what inflames Alberta opinion most is the method by which these decisions, of vital importance to Alberta, were imposed-clearly without consultation and, one must assume, without consideration of the impact the measures will have upon Alberta's capacity to grow.
Whatever disagreement there might be about the things the minister of energy has done, the anger in Alberta today is about the way he has done these things. And the concern for Canada is that the method he has applied here-the method of a bull in a china shop-is a warning of the way in which other provinces might be treated on other issues by other ministers at other times. That warning, sir, is more profound because, while the minister of energy has a special talent for provocation, the style of confrontation which he has adopted toward Alberta is a style which before the last election was becoming a trademark of this government and which apparently now is being renewed.
Sir, no Canadian should need reminding of the diversity of our country. That diversity is the reason we have a

November 8, 1973
Constitution
federal system where provinces and the national government distribute most powers and share others. This federal system was not imposed upon Canada. It grew out of our nature and is the only system which can hope to unite a diverse country and yet allow its individual parts to find their own identity and strength. By the very nature of our country, we are bound to have interests which conflict. That means that a particular obligation lies upon our politicians to try to unite differences, not excite differences. And if that is an obligation upon those of us who sit on the backbenches of parliament, it is an obligation with a particular weight for those who occupy ministerial offices. Yet in this dispute with Alberta that is precisely the obligation which the minister of energy has affronted and ignored.
I want to review for this House the sad record of what has happened, in the name of consultation, on this export tax. But first let me try to make this House understand the particular importance of this question to Alberta. What we are worried about here is not simply revenue, although of course that is important. What we are worried about, as well, is the sense-and we have the sense-that control of resources means control of the future of the province of Alberta. It is very much less a matter of price than it is a matter of future.
We have primarily relied, in the province of Alberta, on primary production, on agriculture. We have the opportunity to industrialize and we have begun to industrialize. But we are working with certain regional disadvantages. Freight rates are one, population distribution is another, market distribution is yet another, the habit of investors to invest in central Canada is another. We have one strong card-petroleum. It provides us with the opportunity to develop petrochemical industries and jobs. Sir, this opportunity would help us to turn the corner and become a strong, industrialized province which would contribute to the industrial strength of the whole of Canada. However, we have no reason for confidence that this goal will be accomplished by Ottawa directing policy, and we have no reason for confidence after looking back at the history of tariffs, at the present discrimination in transportation and at a variety of other matters.
What I should like to do tonight is try to convey a state of mind which it would be folly for other parts of Canada to ignore, just as it would have been folly for other parts of Canada to ignore the state of mind that began manifesting itself in Quebec in the early 1960s. This House should remember that the export tax was one of two barrels which hit Alberta in early September. The other was the prospect that Syncrude might be denied the kind of tax treatment which other oil producers in Alberta would receive and that Syncrude consequently might well be held up. Moreover, sir, the export tax seemed to be a device aimed particularly at Alberta and at Alberta's major resources and not applied, as it might have been, to the resources of other provinces. It was a particular attack on a particular province.
In September, energy ministers of the Alberta and Canadian governments were in Ottawa at a meeting which had been arranged some time previously. The apparent attitude on both sides was conciliatory. The first

item on the agenda was the need for close and continuing consultation. The ministers discussed that first item and agreed to maintain close contact and consult one another thoroughly. The federal minister of energy made the point that in this field events develop quickly and that consultation could not be considered as constituting a right to veto. Naturally, that position was accepted by the representatives of Alberta.
The discussion progressed to other items on the agenda. Then some time between 11 a.m. and noon the federal minister of energy announced that the National Energy Board would be imposing an export tax of about 40 cents and that the announcement would be made publicly later that day. Alberta ministers had no warning that was coming and no opportunity to make comments or suggestions which would materially affect the decision.
Scant minutes after affirming the need for consultation, the federal minister presented Alberta with a fait accompli. That was not consultation. That was mere advice. Any province, treated that way on a matter of such vital interest to its future, would have responded in anger. Indeed, any federal government which enshrined the habit of treating provinces that way would face a breakdown in all of its relations with all of the provinces of Canada. That was the first export tax, the 40-cent tax.
The second act in this charade of consultation began on Monday, October 29-again in Ottawa. Four senior ministers of the government of Alberta came to Ottawa to meet with the federal Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the federal Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner). They were briefed by officials of the Department of External Affairs on developments in the Middle East. They had general discussions concerning plans Ottawa might have for a pipeline to Montreal. They discussed the possibility of staging-in price increases.
On the export tax, the Alberta ministers took the position that since they disagreed with the idea of the tax, they saw no immediate point in discussing how its proceeds might be distributed. It is clear there was no discussion at all of any prospect of an immediate rise in that export tax, and certainly not any discussion of a proposal to more than quadruple the amount. Indeed, the federal minister of energy said that events might develop that would mean an export tax might not have to be imposed. The federal minister indicated to his provincial colleagues that, in his view, the export tax proposal "was not written in stone". The ministers then repaired to a joint press conference at which the provincial minister of intergovernmental affairs went out of his way to make clear Alberta's interest in adopting a "Canada first" position.
Four senior Alberta ministers left those meetings agreed on three clear impressions. Their first impression was that serious consideration was being given to the staging-in of increases. The second impression was that there was now a genuine commitment to consultation on the part of the federal ministers. The third impression was that if there was to be any change at all in the export tax, the change would be in the direction of removing the tax. It is conceivable that one of these ministers might have been wrong, but it is surely stretching credulity to suggest that all four ministers were wrong on all three impressions.
November 8, 1973

Four days later, on Thursday, November 1-a week ago today-the federal minister of energy rose in his place to announce that the export tax had been more than quadrupled. Alberta officials were advised a matter of hours before the public announcement. Again it was advice, not consultation. However, this second case was worse than the first. In the first case, the export tax had come out of the blue. In the second case, it came four days after a meeting in which Alberta ministers believed they received a message that the export tax might go down, or it might go out, but at which no indication at all was given that the tax might go up so exorbitantly.
There might be some members of this House who do not like Albertans. I do not say that there are, but that there might be. That really does not matter because these tactics could be applied to any province, not just Alberta; and on any matter, not just petroleum. I hope that members of this House and of the public generally, no matter how preoccupied they might be about the price of fuel or the extent of foreign ownership of any other extraneous question, will remember that we are dealing here with a method of the application of federal power that could be imposed as arbitrarily upon any province or any interest as it has been upon Alberta.
It is interesting, for example, to conjecture what the response would have been had federal involvement in the financing of higher education been approached in the early 1960s in the spirit which marked the federal imposition this fall of an export tax upon petroleum produced primarily in one province.
I said at the beginning that the purpose of a federal system, and particularly the federal government, must be to unite differences, not inflame them. The reason that is important is that it is easy, in Canada, to inflame differences among regions. Particularly when emotional questions are involved, as emotional questions are involved here, it would be relatively easy to unite most of Canada against one part of Canada. However, that would be a destructive unity which would lead inexorably to the disintegration of the nation.
I utter that caution not simply to my colleagues in this House but also to the press gallery. One problem inherent in our system is the natural tendency of the national press to take Ottawa's view in a dispute with the provinces. That is not due to prejudgment so much as to the fact that journalists are locked in here in day to day contact with one side in a national dispute. I believe it has been harmful to Alberta that this disagreement broke out at roughly the same time that a general election was in progress in Quebec, which meant that several journalists from that province, who have reason to know that Ottawa is not always even-handed in its dealings with the province, were preoccupied at home and thus did not have the opportunity to visit the province and the people of Alberta to learn Alberta's side of this story.
The real tragedy flowing from the methods of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is that it has created an atmosphere of confrontation on a question where federal-provincial co-operation could have prevailed. Alberta wants to co-operate with other provinces and other Canadians to ensure supply and arrange a better price for Canadian consumers. The premier and his ministers have
Constitution
made that clear. They have been calling for some time for a national federal-provincial conference to work out the priorities and the policies that Canada and the provinces might follow to meet the challenges raised by energy questions. However, co-operation is a two-way street. Ottawa must demonstrate a willingness to work with Alberta. That would have been much easier two months ago, before the actions of the minister of energy gave Alberta ample cause to distrust that minister and anyone acting in his name. But it is not impossible to achieve now.
The language of this motion deplores the tactics of confrontation and fear which have marked the approach of this government to federal-provincial relations. Of course we deplore that approach, but we must do more than deplore. We have to turn the practices of this government around and insist, as a parliament, upon an atmosphere of co-operation with the provinces instead of the present atmosphere of confrontation.
It might be more amusing to have the luxury of a full-scale feud between a province and the central government, but that is very literally and clearly a luxury we cannot afford. Not only is there the danger that this atmosphere of confrontation might prolong disagreement about national energy policy; there is also the very real danger that this tactic, if practised continually by the federal government, will lead to a reaction in some regions that will make national unity very difficult to maintain.
However important laws might be in Canada, the thing that finally unites this country is the will to work together. If the federal government indicates by its actions that it would sooner fight than agree, that attitude will become contagious. I hope that the government as a whole, and the minister of energy in particular, will recognize that the leadership they are supposed to offer is leadership in the direction of co-operation, not confrontation.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ENCOURAGE PROVINCIAL CONSULTATION TO REDRAFT THE CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate brought up today by my colleague, the hon. member for Champlain, (Mr. Matte) in introducing this motion, has surely roused the attention of several hon. members who spoke on behalf of their parties, but we noticed there was more emotion than anything else. The Constitution of a country, Mr. Speaker, is a guideline which will be respected if the citizens are happy to live under such a Constitution. Otherwise, it will not be respected. This is about what has been happening, for at least a couple of decades, and we see more and more among the population as the years go by that this Constitution is less and less respected bacause there is a struggle between a centralizing party, the federal party, and the provinces which want to keep their autonomy.
There is competition between those two levels of government, that are seeking to reach the electors by all possible means to flatter the electors with social legislation, legislation on public works, legislation of all kinds in order to reach directly the elector.
That is why, especially during the two World Wars and on the occasion of certain troubles, we saw the federal Liberal party, because after all that was the party in power during those circumstances, use such crises to cen-

November 8, 1973
Constitution
tralize in Ottawa, in collusion with certain provincial governments, powers that had before been reserved to provinces. We saw for instance at the beginning of the 1939 war, the federal government of the time resort to all possible means at its disposal to defeat in Quebec a government that was not a centralizing government, a government that was jealous of its autonomy and they had it replaced by a Liberal party government with a leader who was not too popular, who was not too strong a defender of Quebec's autonomy. So the government took advantage of that opportunity as well as of the war effort to bring to Ottawa a great number of laws that up to that time had been reserved to provinces according to the constitution and it is being said that the provinces agreed to accept such centralization.
Mr. Speaker, an agreement of that kind is precisely the one that prompts citizens to ask themselves questions and to tend more and more to ignore a constitution that bullies them instead of protecting them. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) said at the beginning of his remarks, this afternoon, that since the early days of Confederation, the Liberal party has always acted in the same way in matters of federalism and that is obvious. He does not need to tell us.
As a matter of fact, the Liberal party has been the most centralizing party in Canada and in reply to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, since he referred to the provincial election, I may say that the Quebeckers' vote during the last general election was not a vote of approval of the Canadian constitution, but rather a vote against adventure with a party with a strong socialist tendency, the Parti quebecois. Just a few minutes ago, the Parliamentary Secretary and member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan), who was chairman of the Special Joint Committee on Constitution, also made some remarks on the motion moved by the hon. member for Champlain. He said that it is not the Liberal party which has caused division in this country. Members on the government side recognize therefore that there is some division. But it is mostly in Quebec and because of a certain political party that this exists.
I will reply to the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville that what, among other things, gives strength to the separatist party in Quebec is indeed the centralization of the federal government since Confederation, especially on the occasion of both World Wars and other troubled periods. So, Mr. Speaker, in order to find a fair solution to contitutional problems, whether or not it is admitted certain procedures aiming at the reform of the Constitution are being delayed to amend it, repatriate it, make it more acceptable to Canadians.
The solution which may be given to this problem can only be found by groups of men not dominated by a political doctrine. Ever since the question of the reform of the constitution has been raised, the federal Liberal party has used every conceivable means to dominate the debates and have their own views accepted. Therefore, no wonder each constitutional meeting held both in Ottawa or in Victoria or in any place always fizzled out or has been postponed. An agreement was never reached because a group wanted to dominate all the others.

The provinces also have a right to be heard. The federal government exists thanks to the provinces. The provinces were not born from federalism but the federal government was born from the provinces and more and more we feel the need for readjusting the constitution to our current needs because they are different from those which existed one hundred years back. For instance, at the beginning of confederation the problem of municipalities were minor ones but over the last few years with people concentrating in the urban centres those problems have considerably aggravated. I have also been a member of the committee oh the constitution which held many meetings in Ottawa, which travelled throughout the country to hear people, listen to individuals criticizing the present constitution, offering solutions, and telling us what they hoped to see in the new constitution or in an amended constitution. Everywhere we have met municipal officials who told us how difficult it was for them to administer their municipality because they have a heavier load to carry and because they are increasingly deprived of the means to support this load.
In a recent commercial letter of the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, giving recent statistics for 1972, with a retrospective of the last ten years, it is said that in 1963, municipal revenues in Canada totalled $2,286 million. These revenues increased yearly to reach $5,022 million in 1972. However, municipal government expenses were, in 1963, $2,373 million and have increased yearly to reach $7,165 million in 1972, which is a deficit of $2,143 million in 1972. It means therefore that municipalities, provinces and the federal government must compete on the debenture markets, with stronger governments, to obtain the funds required to balance their budgets. Municipalities, like the provinces and the federal government, are over-indebted, which compels them also to assign too great a part of their budget to debt interest so that the problems, or at least a large part of the problems, that the municipalities face are mainly at the level of the interests they must pay each year to their creditors.
Well, Mr. Speaker, during the sittings of the constitutional committee municipalities asked for increased taxation powers mainly to be able to meet their obligations and that is becoming a struggle, no longer between two parties-the provinces and the federal government-but between three parties-the municipalities, the provinces and the federal government-to have increased access to the incomes of individuals in order to be able to tax them so as to balance their budgets and meet their obligations.
So, Mr. Speaker, in any constitutional reform or amendment those demands on the part of municipalities should be taken into consideration, and not only simply to give them increased taxation powers. They need it, it is true, but in the present system there is no other way out besides the one offered by the Social Credit. And the Liberal Party which has been in power since 1963 lent a deaf ear to the demands and suggestions made by the Creditists in that area. And we are told that the Creditist doctrine or policy on economic matters is no good. But is the present economic policy of the Liberal Party any good?

Not all, of course, as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion just said, and if the economic policy of the Liberal party were sound, the federal government, the provinces and the municipalities as well as the individuals would not be so deep in debt as they are now.
Therefore, this shows that if the Social Credit is not effective, the Liberal party is far from being so itself.
At the committee meetings, a professor of political science and a candidate for the Toronto mayoralty, Mr. Stephen Clarkson, said the following, and I quote:
The municipal government only has a limited power of taxation on real property which constitutes a regressive tax base. We have great problems which are not of our making: immigration, for example, that from the Maritimes. We cannot cope with them and the power is so much centralized in Queen's Park and bureaucracy is so extensive that we cannot accomplish what we feel ought to be done. Therefore, another level of government, should not be created.
For him, such is not the problem, because he feels that everything is centralized in the municipal field, in provincial capitals, and precisely many other municipal representatives have asked that municipalities be recognized as a level of government and as having their say in all essential budgetary measures taken by higher levels of government to balance their budget.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, all we are asking in the motion of my colleague from Champlain is that the federal government urge the provinces to get together in order to amend or redraft the Canadian constitution, and the constitution must exist for the provinces. Therefore, they must have the right to draft this constitution.
Thus, the provinces that have no control over others will be able to draft the necessary sections in order to protect the country against national disturbances by fulfilling the basic aspirations of each province. It is something that the federal government cannot do, because by dictating the sections that must be included in a new constitution, it will seek to have accepted sections which protect the central government of the country, and in protecting itself in this way, it would be difficult to fulfil the basic aspirations of the provinces.
Mr. Speaker, we do not wish, through this motion, to destroy something worthwhile, but we ask the federal government to urge the provinces to meet in order to obtain results, find out what they want and, under the constitution, obtain satisfactory results so that there may exist in every one of the ten provinces a climate of peace in which Canadians from coast to coast will be able and willing to abide by the constitution.
It is in this spirit that this motion was introduced and should be examined while seeking the solutions that all Canadians want.
