speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would simply like to take a few minutes in order to participate in this debate on the motion moved today by a member of the Social Credit Party of Canada.
Constitution
I must admit that I was surprised when I read the motion now before us. I heard recently the comments of this sagacious and shrewd politician, the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) who had predicted the election of a minority government in Quebec following the recent campaign, adding that the party that would suffer the most from this result would be the Creditiste party. I shall not make any comments on the second judgement of the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe as compared to his first, because I am in no position to conclude that his judgement on the second point is as valid or as poor as on the first. But I must regretfully note that this Creditiste motion is not one that could improve the situation of the Social Credit Party of Canada.
I am really surprised at this motion, which reads as follows:
That this House deplores the fact that the government is maintaining the unity of the country through fear, autocracy and oligarchy, and has failed to do anything to encourage the provinces to get together in order to amend or redraft the Canadian constitution, thus protecting the country against national difficulties by meeting the basic aspirations of each province.
And all that in a single sentence. I must confess that after reading this motion over again, I wondered what country it was all about, and what situation it was referring to. It talks about fear, autocracy and oligarchy. I really wonder, looking at my provincial colleagues with whom I had to work during those last years, and looking at the premiers of the various provinces, who are those timid and fearing premiers, those provincial premiers who would be living in daily fear of this federal government, ready to crush them, and which would prevent them from expressing their views on any subject and taking position on matters which come under their own jurisdiction.
There is an old saying that you can die from laughter. I am glad that saying is not entirely accurate, because I fear that there would not be many Creditist members left in this House today.
This motion, Mr. Speaker, also complains that the federal government has failed to do anything to encourage the provinces to get together. Since when do the provinces need the federal government to get together? Frankly, the motion seems incredibly naive, and I would even fear that the provinces would take offence if the federal government were to interfere and try to persuade them, as is suggested here, or to force them to get together in order to amend or redraft the Canadian Constitution.
Surely neither the Constitution nor Canadian politics prevent the provinces from meeting, and indeed they have done so. Let us remember the conference organized under the sponsorship of Mr. Robarts in Toronto, which was called Conference on the Confederation of Tomorrow, and to which the federal government had sent observers. That conference was attended by provincial representations and was convened by the provincial governments. Nothing had prevented them from using this same procedure if they had so wished. The provinces have shown sufficient wisdom and knowledge to realize that if a serious review of the Canadian Constitution was wanted, this could only be done effectively if the provinces would cooperate and act in consultation with the federal government. The result of this conference in Toronto simply was a recommendation that, in cooperation with the federal govern-

November 8, 1973
Constitution
ment, a review of the constitution be undertaken and this is what was done in the following years.
The fact that such a motion is put and the way it is drafted surely indicate a lack of knowledge of federal-provincial relations and a lack of respect for provincial autonomy and for the true power of the provinces in running their own business.
But I would not want to spend my time in a detailed analysis of this motion and demonstrating its inherent weaknesses. I would rather like to say a few words on what really happens in the area of federal-provincial relations.
I often hear people talk about the lack of consultation, in or outside this House, because the federal government reportedly would take unilateral decisions and so on. I think it is important to underline once again, and to repeat it constantly, that consultations do not give any right of veto and that the federal government is the government responsible for the national interest in the areas under its jurisdiction. Even if the federal government has everything to gain by regular and frequent consultations with provincial governments when there is a decision of national interest to take which is under its jurisdiction, the federal government must finally take the decision, even if this decision is not welcomed by all the provinces of Canada.
In a similar way, this is also true in the case of the provinces. I think it is their interest to consult with the federal government in many areas for which they are responsible and they should do it more often. I have no hesitation in saying that the federal government consults with the provinces a hundred times more in the areas under its jurisdiction than do the provinces in the areas under their own jurisdiction.
However this having been said, we often consult the provinces and I will give some details on that particular subject in a few minutes. However, once again, when a discussion takes place, it rests with the federal government to take decisions in matters under its jurisdiction and if any province is not satisfied with such decisions, it is unfortunate but just the same some government must be responsible for the national interest.
When the media, the opposition, the members of the government or provincial politicians then intervene and deplore the fact that the federal government acts unilaterally and without consultation, as they often suggest, I maintain once again that they are mistaken. There has been some consultation, but the government has assumed its responsibility for which it must answer to the House and to the Canadian people, but not to the provincial governments.
When I heard the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) this afternoon say that a conservative federal government would proceed through consultation and on a collegial basis, I believe he was introducing a concept of federal-provincial collegial government in matters of federal-provincial relations. Well, in this country, a federal government that would suggest a form of collegial government with the provinces would be deluding the people and moreover ruin the constitution.

There have been consultations. I shall refer to the first year of the progressive conservative government during the last 20 or 30 years. In 1957, at the ministerial level, five meetings took place with the provinces. At the official level, for a whole year there were 59, thus making a total of 64.
This means that in 1967, that is 10 years later, we had 14 meetings at the ministerial level and 105 at the official level for a total of 119. Three years later, in 1970, there were 18 meetings at the ministerial level, one and a half per month on the average, and 200 at the official level, for a total of 220, between the federal and provincial governments.
There has been a steady increase which keeps on. Not one day goes by that a meeting between the federal government and the provinces is not held in this country. Whether it be at the senior official or minister level, whether they be bilateral or multilateral meetings, or whether visits in the provinces or by provincial representatives to Ottawa.
Even more important, over recent years and even quite recently, this consultation process has been extended through the initiative of the federal government in the area of tripartite meetings to which municipalities were invited to participate.
We know also that recently a very successful conference, a three-level meeting took place in Edmonton in which the minister responsible for urban affairs took part.
That is what really happened and what is always going on without any startling statements, without getting in the headlines. But what we will find in the headlines will be the story of the conference or meeting resulting in deep disagreement. We rarely hear about the current meetings where the federal and provincial governments make progress and come to an agreement.
It is unfortunate that there is a tendency to feature exclusively stumbling blocks, difficulties and points of disagreement. This is what is happening in the field of federal-provincial relations. However I could talk more in detail about my own departments. For instance, we undertook this year with the provinces a review of social security and this has already brought about three meetings of welfare ministers and several meetings of senior officials.
Before these meetings, the federal government submitted a working paper that received the unanimous endorsement of the provinces. We had regular meetings once more with the provinces and ministers and to date we have obtained unanimous assent on all points which have been discussed. This will not necessarily go on because there will certainly be some disagreements either among the provinces themselves, between the federal government and the provinces or some of them. This is only natural and we would be wrong to be shocked. To imagine that the motion presented by the Creditist party to convene a meeting of the provinces where they would reach an agreement which would be impossible if the federal government were present is nothing but a dream and a complete lack of understanding of the way in which this country operates.
In the area of energy which has been mentioned before, I only need to mention the example of the relationship
November 8, 1973

between Alberta and Ontario, two governments of the same party, which were prepared to go before the courts to settle their dispute concerning energy. We know what happened in the field of feed grains and about the so-called "Chicken war", in Canada. The federal government was not directly involved; there was direct confrontation between the provinces of Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec and the Maritimes and once more, the federal government had nothing to do with it.
The provinces, therefore should meet together and reach an agreement that the federal government would only endorse. Once more, this means living in a world that does not exist and that is not Canada as it exists at the present time.
I referred to social security. I will deal with another matter on which no agreement was reached to date, that of health. For three years, discussions have been held at senior officials level with provinces, to come to a new financing formula in the area of health, a formula designed to secure larger flexibility in the administration of health services, for provinces in particular. That formula was changed several times during the discussions, and was finally presented to health and finance ministers during a conference that was held last year in Ottawa.
Finally, no agreement was reached on the formula that was proposed and during the premiers' conference, a new formula was proposed, considered by the provinces, but was finally rejected. There is nothing to be ashamed of.
' Many provinces had expressed an interest for such or such aspect, and the fact that they finally preferred the present system to another does not authorize them to conclude that there is autocracy or oligarchy-whatever the name they choose to call it-on the part of the federal government; but it is not fear, as stated in the motion, which encouraged the provinces to reject the federal proposal. In fact, they decided that it was not in their interest to accept the proposed formula. A while ago, the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe indicated that his party .would propose a transfer of resources, together with a transfer of tax power, while taking equalization payments into account. I urge him to take cognizance of the proposal which the federal government, through its Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), made in the spring at the last meeting of provincial premiers. He will then realize that he did not invent the moon, for this very proposal has already been made to and refused by the premiers. They deemed it unsatisfactory on the financial level, which is nothing new.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to use more of the House's time. I merely wish to emphasize again that the area of federal provincial relations is extremely complex-

speechtext:
I have a lot to say, but I shall not say it all tonight. As a point of departure I should like to take the concluding remarks of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde). These were to the effect that one of the manifestations of a healthy federal system is the existence of tensions within that system. He said that as soon as the tensions and problems cease to exist, it means that the federal system has in effect died either by the absorption, total and complete, of the provinces by the national government or the virtual total destruction and rendering ineffective of the federal government by the provinces. The minister put it much more elegantly and eloquently, but I think that is an accurate summary of his remarks.
I think what characterizes federal-provincial relations to me is not autocracy and oligarchy, as suggested by the motion, so much as confusion. I think the minister would be one of the first to admit, even taking his view as the point of departure, that tensions will always exist withip a federal state and that they are signs of vitality within the federal state; they are signs of experimentation and signs of attempts to adapt to new situations and changes in values. Therefore, it is desirable that we restructure our constitution to some extent with the end in view of removing to the extent possible the occasions for confusion in relations between the provinces and the federal government. It is necessary to reduce the confusion and ambiguities in the constitution so as to remove some of the causes of frustration and anger, as opposed to tension, that we heard expressed by hon. members from Alberta and Quebec who spoke this evening.
It is not so important to me that the constitution accurately define whether this country is to move toward centralization or decentralization, because I think if the constitution is going to serve the needs of the country it has to be able to move either way as the needs and locus of power in the country and values of the country change.
One of the ways to accomplish that objective is to alter our division of powers. At the moment, the division of power is in three lists. There is a list of exclusive federal powers and a list of exclusive provincial powers. Both of these sections have items which are not particularly well defined. There is also a very short list of three or four areas of concurrent jurisdiction. It would seem to me that we could overcome a good deal of the difficulty that we encounter in this country in permitting regions to adapt their relationships to the federal government in a manner which will enable the government to meet the needs of the people, by modifying our allocation of powers so that we, in effect, have four lists of powers. There would be a rather short list of exclusive federal powers such as

defence, international affairs, monetary policy, customs tariffs, and that sort of thing; then a rather short list of exclusive provincial powers, and a fairly extensive list of concurrent powers in which the paramountcy of federal or provincial power would be indicated in each case. There would also be another list where powers could be delegated from one level to another on the basis of bilateral agreement.
I feel this would meet the needs and shifts of balance of power in the country. There are times when a country needs stronger central direction and others when it is better decentralized. I think that such a normal political process has to be accommodated in the constitution. The delegation of powers from the federal government to the provinces, or vice versa, on a bilateral basis would accommodate that process and reduce the causes of frustration that presently exist as opposed to what are normal healthy tensions.
My point in rising tonight was not to suggest specific changes to the current constitution of Canada. My colleague the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), and also the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather), during the course of debate suggested some areas which require change. They made specific suggestions and argued them very cogently, urging the government to proceed with them. I do not want to repeat their arguments and I do not want to refer to the specific areas that I think need change. What I really want to do tonight, Mr. Speaker, is to argue very strongly that now is a most propitious time to get on with the job of attempting to reach some kind of agreement on the kind of constitution we want-to bring it to Canada, to have it repatriated, and to complete the process which was begun a long time ago of modifying our constitution and deciding upon an amendment formula.
I do not think it is good enough for the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to say that he is willing to embark upon this adventure when the provinces indicate to him that they want to undertake the exercise once again. As the minister who just spoke so properly pointed out, we are here as a national parliament to look after the national interests of Canada. The government is there to look after national interests. I think it is in the national interest that we complete this exercise.
Even if there is some reluctance on the part of the provinces at the moment, or a simple lack of interest, it is up to the federal government to provide the leadership necessary to get the process under way. I think now is a propitious time. There is a desire on the part of the people of Canada to have the constitution repatriated. This desire became obvious when, as a member of the joint Senate and House of Commons Committee on the Constitution, I travelled about the country and saw the interest generated by the committee in what might have been considered a dry, academic subject. This apparent desire to do something about the constitution is manifest in the fact that such a large measure of agreement was possible at Victoria in 1971 when the provinces and the federal government met. I would like to see the exercise completed.
What argues most strongly that we should try to complete this exercise at this point is that we are now, despite the current outrage of the representatives from Alberta,
November 8, 1973

and despite the almost universal disquiet on the part of those representing Quebec about the results of the election there, in a period of relative stability. One of the things which I suggest to hon. members has contributed to our failure to complete the exercise of redrafting our constitution, to the extent it needs reform, and deciding on the amendment formula and bringing it to Canada, is the fact that the exercise has normally been pursued during periods of crisis, rapid change, shifts in value or of the locus of power in this country.
These are times when the tolerance of ambiguity on the part of governments is vastly reduced. At such times, if they are to change the constitution they want every "i" dotted and every "t" crossed. Because the country is in the process of change, a government is not willing to take a chance on the possibility of an error being absolved and corrected by the unwritten part of our constitution, which is really the most important part. Governments are not willing to take that chance because they think there might be something unalterable in the written part of the constitution. That is how governments think in critical periods when they are most afraid to take risks.
At this point in time the country is relatively stable. Perhaps there will be a willingness to take that kind of risk on the part of participating governments. Perhaps it is really worth while pursuing that idea now.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate. I, along with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), read the motion with great interest. I suggest that the minister, being a Queen's Counsel of the bar of the province of Quebec, has perhaps taken a somewhat legalistic approach to this issue which the Social Credit party has brought to the attention of the House.
I do not intend to become involved in what I consider to be a little confrontation within this chamber with respect to events of a week or so ago in one of the provinces of Canada. I merely say to the minister that perhaps the motion before the House expresses an attitude to something that is essential to confederation. By implication it deals, I submit, with the relationship between the federal government and all the provinces of Canada. It expresses an attitude that this debate shows has been developing in the country. That attitude is that this government, for better or worse, whether with malice aforethought or without, has tended to shake the foundations of the belief that it is truly interested in the federal system. One important element of this system involves consultation.
The hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark) spoke eloquently about the problems of Alberta and the feelings of the people of that province. Let us talk about the people of Alberta. I suppose that if we substituted for oil any commodity of concern to other provinces of Canada-let us say we were talking about something of concern to the province of Ontario, Quebec, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick or any other region-we would
Constitution
find, if the people of the province had been treated as the people of Alberta have been treated, that they would react in exactly the same way as the people of Alberta have reacted. It is to that feeling that the motion of the Credi-tistes is directed. In that sense, our embarking upon this debate is healthy for us.
We are considering in the House the entire question of foreign ownership. The members of my party, in their discussions on the matter, have not forgotten that an essential ingredient is leadership by the federal government. They have attempted to pay more than lip service to the idea that there must be provincial consultation. That matter is not one of mere tokenism. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) said, as the government has said, that this is not going to happen under the legislation to which I have just alluded.
A few weeks ago in Edmonton there was a conference on northern affairs and the question of revenue sharing arose. In the result, some provinces were in favour of the concept-the province of Ontario and others-and some were against it. There was an issue that could be discussed. Yet how did the government react? The minister responsible for urban affairs turned thumbs down on the idea, or used the federal veto, to use the words of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, with respect to any discussion on revenue sharing as between the provinces and the federal government. The government even turned down any discussion on the subject. This attitude is creeping into many areas, and we are in danger of losing sight of what has traditionally been and remains an essential part of our federalism, that is, consultation.
According to what I read about the attitude of the provinces and what I hear from public men in the provinces, the provinces do not want the veto, as the Minister of National Health and Welfare suggested the other day. They want realistic consultation between provincial governments, which are responsible to the people in the provinces, and the national government which is responsible to the whole country. I suppose the message we can derive from this debate is that we must treat confederation as a delicate flower. It is delicate and, like a flower, must be gently treated. You must not hack at it with a hoe or a shovel. Our confederation must be handled with gentle and understanding hands.
I think we should look at this matter in the context of federal-provincial conferences. Some have been successful, others unsuccessful. The successful conferences have been those in which the parties felt there was a reasonable attitude of co-operation. The principals at the conference, the provinces and the federal government, accepted the need fo. co-operation. They felt that their own interests would not be overlooked or treated lightly.
The conferences that have been unsuccessful, and there have been many, have been those in which there was conflict and confrontation, invited perhaps for political purposes. In any event, one or more of the principals felt threatened at such conferences. We must not forget that our people want co-operation when these discussions go on.

There is concern about this consultation and I feel that much attention is paid to it. In fact, numerous comments have been made about the importance of preliminary consultations with the provinces whatever the level and legislation to be amended.
It is my opinion that we will never pay too much attention to this question and that we will never insist too much on having the minister responsible or the government take measures so that the provinces will be consulted as much as possible.
There were also references to the reasons that seemed unacceptable to certain provinces. Mention was made of Alberta and Quebec. I think that certain provinces are not altogether happy with the present system. There have been reasons for this and I believe it is fair to discuss them. There was even criticism of the last provincial election campaign in Quebec.
Now I believe that if one is surprised to learn today that 30 per cent of the Quebeckers do not believe in federalism

anymore, I think one must recall that Mr. Gerard Filion spoke 30 years ago about economical separatism and that was due to the eastern policy on feed grain. I hasten to mention the fact in order to show those who are trying to understand that it is surely not Quebec that invented separatism, considering the fact that the province of Quebec lost $300 million on account of that feed grain policy that has been discriminatory for 30 years. But it seems to me that the government is now trying to correct that injustice. I know it is hard for the minister to do it for he is very busy and hard-pressed by western organizations. As a matter of fact, I believe he wants at last to do justice to all Canadian producers.
I think that unrest was due to a certain lack of consultation and to certain intrusions on the part of the federal government into provincial administration. But for this purpose I must refer to the two administrations that governed Canada.
Therefore, when referring to this problem, one realizes today that in Quebec, a great number of people are losing faith in federalism and often wonder why. But one can be delighted by the result of the provincial election.
As far as the economic stability of the province of Quebec is concerned, the answer was clear and it will enable Quebec to avoid this kind of slackening that takes place when a government is beaten, whether blue or red. There is always some slackening when we speak of changing a system. But in the circumstances, I am delighted by the specific answer that many citizens of Quebec and of Canada were anxiously waiting for.
We had well defined options, on both sides. Although the Parti Quebecois had submitted an option that was debated and debatable, it did so clearly and the people made their decision. But I urge hon. members not to forget the high proportion of French-speaking people who reject today the present system, because it might be dangerous to rejoice blindly when one considers that almost 38 per cent against 46 per cent of the voters rejected this system. Now, the answer was for Quebec to remain within confederation. For my part, I have never recommended the separation of Quebec, on the contrary, but it is my duty as a Quebec member to uphold my interests, as it is the duty of Newfoundland or Alberta members to uphold theirs.
When those suggestions can be made objectively, I think that we shall have a better chance of reaching our common goal. While for many people in Quebec, and even in Canada, the answer was clear, I hope that with the power it has received, the newly elected government will be more demanding as regards some of the powers it needs. The Laurendeau-Dunton Commission and the Committee on the Constitution have recognized, as we all know, that Quebec is the nucleus of the French-

Canadian nation, and that it holds a special place in Canada because of its largely French-speaking population.

NATIONAL DEFENCE-INQUIRY AS TO DECISION ON REPLACEMENT FOR ARGUS AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in this adjournment debate on a replacement for the Argus. I want to be kind to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson), who I think is sincerely trying to come to a decision on this question. However, there have been other sincere ministers of defence during the past five years-which some Canadians think have been five years too long-of the Trudeau government. There have been four different ministers of defence during these five years, and I am afraid that in a constructive but rather critical way one could say that a review of the parliamentary returns to questions raised about replacing the Argus shows a rather sad catalogue of confusion and uncertainty in Department of National Defence planning.
With four ministers in five years, is it any wonder that those who served, and who served well, in the armed services are themselves confused about the role they are supposed to play in defence policy? I intend to review, in the short time available to me, those parliamentary returns which began when the issue of the Argus was first raised. I am talking about five squadrons, involving 32 aircraft which have been in use really since 1958. They have been operating almost on a daily basis somewhere in the skies over Canada, except when grounded for weather reasons or sometimes because of mechanical breakdown, for 15 years. Even though it is a different mode of transportation, how many of us are using a 15-year old car with the same confidence as when we first purchased it? The airframes were first designed for 10,000 air hours. Because of procrastination and indecision, the airframe lifespan was revised to 19,000 hours. Some of the aircraft are beginning to approach this extended airframe life.
November 8, 1973

I do not have time tonight to debate defence policy in all its aspects, but to set the record straight it was on March 17, 1969, as reported at page 6681 of Hansard, when the first recorded question that I have been able to find dealing with the Argus was asked by the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall). He asked:
Is the DND presently giving active consideration to the question
of a follow-on replacement aircraft for the Argus presently in
use by Maritime Command?
The Hon. Leo Cadieux, then minister of defence, replied, "Yes". On May 7, 1969, as reported at page 8419 of Hansard, in reply to a written question from the same member for Dartmouth-Halifax East, the parliamentary secretary to the minister replied:
No decision will be made until phase II of the defence review has been completed.
On June 26, 1970, as reported at page 8643, the Hon. Leo Cadieux, replying to the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. MacLean), said:
We have conducted an evaluation of prototypes of new aircraft that could eventually replace the Argus aircraft, if the government so authorizes DND ... it will be later than October when these studies are completed .. . There are many considerations involved. The fundamental decision is as to whether we will make a replacement at this time . . . The decision will not be a decision of the Minister of National Defence, it will be a decision by the government, and no doubt all the relevant factors pertaining to it will be considered.
Then on September 29, 1971, as reported at page 8279, the new minister of defence, the now Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald), replying to a question from the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Rowland), said this:
I should remind the hon. member that as well as the option of replacing the Argus, there is the option of refitting it for future use.
Then on March 28, 1972, as reported at page 1211 of Hansard, the next minister of national defence, the Hon. E. J. Benson, in replying to a question from me, said:
If my hon. friend would look at what I have said with regard to the Argus and Tracker aircraft, he would understand that the question of their replacement is presently being studied and a report is expected in the very near future.
Then on June 16, 1972, as reported at page 3205, I asked this question:
When will there be a decision on the Argus replacement?
Mr. Benson replied:
The matter is being studied, Mr. Speaker.
On February 5, 1973, as recorded at page 946 of Hansard, the present Minister of National Defence, in reply to a question from myself, said:
The government has decided to replace the Argus but we have not yet made a decision as to the type of aircraft to be ordered. We have sent out letters to five airplane manufacturers inviting them to make proposals against our specifications and we have requested that these proposals be in our hands by March 21 . . . We will also be looking at the regional aspects and, hopefully, this major purchase will bring industrial benefit to all regions of Canada.
Then on October 17 of this year, as recorded at pages 6955 and 6956 of Hansard, again in a reply to a question from me, the Minister of National Defence said:
Adjournment Debate
We will be entering the contract definition phase in the near future. I expect to make a recommendation to cabinet within the next two or three weeks.
I do not have the time now to review all those answers, Mr. Speaker. However, it has been 55 months and 22 days-more than four and a half years-since the first question was asked in this House about the status of the aircraft. Also, the minister well knows, from reviewing the file, that questions were also asked in committee before that of a fifth minister of national defence who is now the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) sitting on this side of the House. In all that time there still has not been a decision.
Mr. Speaker, I fully appreciate the complexity of the decision. However, in closing-because my time is just about finished, according to the rules governing this proceeding-I say that there must be a decision so that the contract specifications can go to the main bidders, if it is confined to that, and so that the people of Canada, and especially the servicemen of Canada who are vitally involved in this project, can be informed and will have some reassurance about their future prospects. Further procrastination cannot be allowed to play with the lives of the men who are flying the Argus aircraft-and we will be reaching that stage very soon.

Because of that situation I asked whether the Minister of Transport was considering bringing into the negotiations, before the agreement is finally signed, the question of providing the province of Saskatchewan with an air route out of Regina or Saskatoon into the American market. That is the topic which I wish to pursue.
An analysis of the latest bilateral proposal reveals that the province of Saskatchewan was not included in the proposed route configurations. This is the result of unilateral decision-making on the part of the federal government. The federal government has had every opportunity to learn at first hand the need for direct air access to the United States. Top representatives of the Ministry of Transport and Air Canada were in attendance at the provincial transportation conference held in Saskatoon on March 22, 1973, when the Premier of Saskatchewan stated:
Historically, Saskatchewan governments have supported Air Canada as the sole regional and transcontinental air carrier. We opposed Air Canada divesting itself of its regional role as we felt, I think, that if you have a monopoly in a province, you have certain responsibilities to maintain adequate levels of service.
Because Saskatchewan is the only province in the west with only one class I carrier, with no north-south jet service and with no international connections, who can blame us if we feel disadvantaged and if we demand adequate air service. Well we don't feel a bit backward in this regard and I can advise Mr. Baldwin he will hear all about it tomorrow.
A wide-ranging discussion which followed on international air transportation made little impression on the former Air Canada president, the director general of civil aviation and the executive director of the air transport committee, all of whom were in attendance and participated in the discussion.
Saskatchewan has not and, if the recent bilateral proposal is ratified, will not have a direct air route to the United States for some time. Saskatchewan requirements for direct air connections with the United States have been pointed out to federal authorities on several occasions in the past. The province's requirements for a U.S. air connection are, in order of priority: first, a direct route to Minneapolis from Regina; second, a direct route to Denver and access to the southwestern United States from Regina or Saskatoon. It is felt that a direct routing to Minneapolis and Chicago is required because of the needs

of business, agriculture, farm implement dealers and educational institutions, and also because of the two-way flow of tourist traffic. More specifically, direct air freight and air express service is clearly needed.
An analysis of the origin and destination statistics from Vancouver, Calgary and Regina to Minneapolis, from which centres there is no direct air contact, reveal the following: the statistics show that in 1972, 9,325 passengers travelled between these points and Minneapolis. Of these, 3,500 originated in or were destined to Vancouver and would certainly have travelled via Seattle.
Calgary passengers have the option of travelling south by Western Airlines or travelling to Winnipeg and connecting with North West Orient Airlines. Similarly, in 1972 the statistics indicate that 21,000 people travelled between Toronto and Minneapolis although there is no direct connection. The direct route of Vancouver to Calgary which would pick up Edmonton traffic, Regina, which would pick up Saskatoon traffic, and Minneapolis- Toronto showed a total passenger movement in 1972 of 30,280, all handled by American airlines as there are no direct Canadian connections. If Winnipeg-Minneapolis is included, 12,520 passengers can be added to this figure, for a total of 43,000 passengers.
Saskatchewan recommended to the Minister of Transport that every effort be made to negotiate a route by a Canadian carrier, namely, Vancouver, Calgary, Regina, Minneapolis, Toronto. Such a route would give Toronto direct access to Minneapolis by a Canadian carrier, a direct route from Regina to Minneapolis-a most urgent need at this time-a one-stop flight from Calgary, and would result in a diversion of much of the traffic now being handled from Vancouver via Seattle. It is considered that this route effectively rebuts the claims of the officials of the Ministry of Transport that a Regina-Minneapolis link is uneconomic and will probably be uneconomic into the 1980s.
Mr. Speaker, if the government were to follow this line, they would find that with a growth factor of 8 per cent- which is below the national average-the figures over the next six years would show the viability of Saskatchewan's proposal to be most impressive. Saskatchewan wonders why such a route configuration was never considered by the Department of Transport, Air Canada or the negotiating team.
Second in importance to a Minneapolis connection is one to Denver. Mr. Speaker, I would follow that up if I had the time to do so. May I conclude by saying that Saskatchewan is of the opinion that the proposed Vancouver or Calgary, Regina, Minneapolis, Toronto routing is clearly feasible, and that if this routing cannot be negotiated into the current bilateral proposal there should at least be provision made in the agreement for consideration of this routing before the next round of formal bilateral route negotiation.
This is the position of the government of the province of Saskatchewan respecting a direct route on a north-south basis. It is supported by the people of Saskatchewan, the mayor of Regina, the city of Regina, the Regina Chamber of Commerce, the Saskatchewan Motor Club world travel department, Kramer Tractor Limited, the manager of John Deere Limited, the president of Roll-O-Flex (1970) Limit-

speakeroldname: Mr. Joseph-Philippe Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-BILATERAL AGREEMENT ON ROUTES WITH UNITED STATES-POSSIBLE RENEGOTIATION OF ONE ROUTE FOR SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a personal basis, I believe the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Knight) could add my name to the others, for the record. Speaking on behalf of the department, the study presented by the Attorney General of Saskatchewan on October 19 dealing with the need for direct air service between Saskatchewan and the United States contains some very useful information on the feasibility of establishing a Vancouver or Calgary, Regina, Minneapolis, Toronto route, particularly by 1978, or as a second priority a north-south route linking Regina or Saskatoon to Denver.
Apart from the question of public interest, any new route would require the support of an airline willing to operate it before the government could put forward a formal proposal for negotiations. The problem here is how soon would traffic between Regina and Minneapolis or Denver develop to a point where direct air service would be justified from the airline's standpoint? As the minister indicated earlier, it would be difficult at this time to relate or hold up the entire route agreement on the question only of a transborder route between Saskatchewan and a U.S. point. In any event, negotiations at the next round of bilateral talks will certainly take the interests of Saskatchewan into full consideration.
In the meantime, we might take advantage of the provisions of a 1966 exchange of notes between Canada and the U.S. relating to local and regional air services. Under these provisions, if a Canadian or U.S. carrier is interested in operating a local or regional-type route such as Regina-Minot or Regina-Great Falls, arrangements could be made by aeronautical authorities without renegotiating the whole route agreement.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: AIRPORTS-PICKERING-COMPETENCE OF BOARD OF INQUIRY TO STUDY NEED AND LOCATION
AIRPORTS-PICKERING-COMPETENCE OF BOARD OF INQUIRY TO STUDY NEED AND LOCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is imperative that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mar-chand) enlarge the terms of reference for the board of examiners that is to study the proposed Pickering airport. On June 22 I asked the minister whether he was directing the proposed board to study the question of airport need. He replied that the board had been constituted in order to allow interested parties to make representations and appear before it. That is the point I seek to make tonight. The board is fundamentally a passive body, when it should be an active, initiating body.
As recently as October 25, according to a news release which I have in my hand, the terms of reference of that board were revised. Fundamentally, the character of the board remained the same as before. It is still, basically, a passive organization rather than an active one. It is fundamentally an organization for receiving opinions rather than seeking them. That might be justified in some circumstances but not in those surrounding the proposal
Adjournment Debate
regarding Pickering airport. I say that because of the public controversy which this proposal has stimulated.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was in Scarborough in March, 1972, he told a large audience of electors that if 51 per cent of the people in the area affected by this airport were opposed to its construction, the government would not force it upon them. He did not say how he would find out that 51 per cent were opposed; nevertheless, he made that commitment. According to a newspaper survey taken by a Toronto daily last spring, 56 per cent of the Toronto people interviewed do not want this airport. Only 26 per cent of those interviewed spoke in favour of it.
As there is such evident opposition to this airport, it is absolutely mandatory on the part of the government to instruct, authorize and finance this board in such a way that it will seek to deal more actively with the fundamental questions that concern the people of the area. It should ask, namely: Does the public want Pickering airport? Should the airport be built at this particular location?
Let me give one further reason why it is absolutely necessary for a board of examination to do this work. Citizens groups should not do it for them. A recent study of the land to be used for this proposed airport shows that it is almost all prime agricultural soil. At a time of world food shortages it is surely unconscionable to take out of production land that should be used to grow food. In the study by two members of the Department of Land Resource Science, University of Guelph, the following claim is made:
Agricultural land is the world's most valuable resource . . .
To lose the best land is to lose the capacity to feed and trade . . .
In the years from 1951 to 1966 the farm population in southern Ontario and the number of farms declined by 26.3 and 24 per cent respectively.
Surely, in light of that trend, it is incumbent on the government to reverse direction and not, as it proposes, to pave over still more prime farmland. While such a decision might have been excusable a few years ago, it cannot be excusable any longer. We are living in a time of nutritional crisis, and it is a time for the government to act. Here, surely, is an opportunity for action. The government should instruct and fund the board of examination to authorize studies on all aspects of the basic question, which is: Should this land be diverted from food production to air transportation?
According to the report referred to, "Pickering township is capable of supporting a productive agricultural industry on a continuing basis." If that is so, and scientific opinion so concludes, the government cannot rightly take this land out of food production unless there are overwhelming reasons to justify it. That alone should require the board of examination to take the initiative instead of waiting for citizens to do its work.
In Chicago, O'Hare Airport handles seven times the traffic which Malton handles, yet O'Hare officials say that no expansion is planned until 1990 despite that airport being about the same size as Malton: it has about the same number of acres. Can we justify taking over farmland when it is clear that Malton could get us by for another 20 years? At a time when fuel shortages are causing some airlines to reduce flights, should we plan an airport expansion program as though there is no fuel crisis, no possibili-

ty that there will be a fall-off in airline use, and do so at the price of removing 17,000 acres from food production?
As we are faced by the challenge that confronts us at a time of world food shortage and the fact that we are in danger of interfering with prime agricultural land, the government is under the absolute obligation to further enlarge the terms of reference of this board so that it may carry out adequate studies. It should initiate, fund and conclude these studies in such a way that the public will be satisfied that if an airport is to be built it is absolutely the only option open to the government. Otherwise, the government cannot justly go ahead with its proposal.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joseph-Philippe Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AIRPORTS-PICKERING-COMPETENCE OF BOARD OF INQUIRY TO STUDY NEED AND LOCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows as well as I what the inquiry will do, but I will answer his question. On June 22 when the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. Stackhouse) put his original question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), his concern was that the airport inquiry commission would not have the power to study need and location.
Since that date the commissioners have been appointed and the terms of reference they have been given specifically relate to need and location, among other factors, allowing them the very broadest terms of reference. I very seldom read anything into the record on the "late show", but to put the record straight I would like to read the pertinent parts of the terms of reference. The commissioners will:
-receive and record new evidence, if available, and, if available and adduced, to report on such new evidence in response to the following questions:
(a)	respecting need,
(i)	is there any new evidence as to what is the expected maximum passenger traffic volume in the domestic, transborder and international air traffic markets for the year 1980 and
what are the best estimates of rates of growth beyond 1980, and
(ii)	is there any new evidence that Toronto International Airport, Malton, can be expanded or reconfigured, within present boundaries, to meet all reasonable needs, having regard to runway capacity, ground access, terminal capacity and the number of people affected by disturbance from flight operations for the period up to 1980, 1990 and 2000:
(b)	respecting location,
is there any new evidence to prove that the site near Pickering, Ontario is not suitable for the new international airport for the central Ontario market having regard to
(i)	disturbance from flight operations,
(ii)	passenger convenience,
(iii)	regional economic effect,
(iv)	total environmental effect, positive and negative, and
(v)	facilities required, including related infrastructures such as roads, railways, guideways and helicopter facilities, and
(c)	generally, is there any new evidence of any relevant factor that has not been considered by the Government of Canada, such, for example, as established facts on technology or travel habits, that may appear to affect any decision of the Government of Canada taken to date.
This is what the board has been given to study. I am sure all members have a copy of the authority given to the board. The commission is headed by Mr. Justice Hugh F. Gibson, of the Federal Court of Canada. These are not just fly-by-night fellows who have been appointed. Members are former metro Toronto planning commissioner Murray V. Jones, president of Murray V. Jones and Associates Ltd., and Dr. Howard Petch, vice-president (academic) of the University of Waterloo and former member of the Science Council of Canada. This is a distinguished group of men whose integrity and independence are beyond challenge.
